content: With Anthropic's long-awaited IPO set to kick off Thursday, luxury home sellers across the country are dangling an unusual offer to its employees: Trade your Anthropic equity for a multimillion-dollar home, and — depending on the address — a radically different commute. With luxury homes proving harder to move in a challenging real estate market, sellers are getting creative about finding buyers, and the impending IPO has put a pool of prospective homeowners on their radar. At its targeted $1.4 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be one of the world's most valuable companies despite having only 5,300 employees. For workers with meaningful equity, the IPO could turn their paper fortunes into something they could touch and live in. Here are three properties Anthropic employees could buy directly with their shares — unless they want to stake their entire fortune on AI — and the commutes that come with them. The 1210 Chickory Lane mansion in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, listed for $29,995,000, may be the most valuable property yet to accept equity from an AI company as payment. The newly built five-bedroom estate sits at the end of a quiet path, with floor-to-ceiling glass, an infinity pool, and a rooftop bar offering 270-degree views from downtown Los Angeles to the Pacific. Designed by IR Architects and Colossal Properties, it also includes a home theater, wine room, gym, sauna, chef's kitchen, four-car garage, and an elevator. The closest Anthropic office to the property, however, is a five-hour drive away in San Francisco. Ideal for those who interpret RTO as a test of personal endurance. Phillip Braunstein, the owner of the property and a developer, told Business Insider that he offered to trade the house for equity in Anthropic because the local market for luxury homes was soft, especially after a proposed billionaire tax sparked talk of moving among those who could afford such a home. "I believe the business behind the demand for intelligence may hit road bumps, but overall it's going to be up and to the right," Braunstein said. "So I think that even if there was a correction and the shares became worth less than what I had set the dollar amount of the house for, over time they would be worth multiples of that amount in the long enough timeframe," Braunstein added. Philip said he uses AI extensively in his own life, from experimenting with stock-trading tools to automating routine tasks. He said an AI agent now handles his bill payments, including his mortgage and utility bills. "I would say the views are probably number one," Braunstein said of his favorite features of the house. "There's also 110 feet of glass that's motorized. Even though it's very modern, it's also very warm-feeling. You feel tucked in when you go down into the house." Sebastian Sagar, a finance professional now based in Florida, previously told Business Insider that he listed his Tribeca apartment at 415 Washington Street for $6.25 million and would prefer payment in Anthropic shares. The apartment features a patio overlooking the neighborhood, a kitchen with dark marble countertops, and oversize windows. Sagar said he bought the property for about $7 million in late 2024 and first listed it in June 2025. He has since cut the asking price and switched brokers. The idea of swapping the apartment for Anthropic stock came after Sagar learned that the AI company was opening an office at 330 Hudson Street, roughly a 10-minute walk away. Close enough that a delayed elevator is the only transit disruption worth discussing. A Williamsburg seller is asking $5.99 million for their Brooklyn home and told Business Insider they will accept bitcoin or vested Anthropic shares as payment. The four-bedroom home sits in a private mews beside Domino Park. It has three full baths, two powder rooms, a finished basement, and a garage with EV charging. Features include a landscaped garden, a rooftop deck with Manhattan skyline views, white oak floors, and a full-floor living room with a gas fireplace. The seller, who has lived in the neighborhood for a decade and uses Anthropic's products daily, said in a statement to Business Insider in June that news of the company's confidential IPO filing prompted them to add shares as an option. This one is a commuter's choose-your-own-adventure: subway, ferry, bike, or a view that makes calling in sick unusually tempting. Jump to

After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since. For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks. Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures. Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.) Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries. Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives. Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there. Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit. At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.) Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report. “Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz says. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says. A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.” Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her. Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the company offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him. Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest company in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it. Updated: 11/19/2026 12:13 p.m. EST This story has been updated to include Anthropic's market debut performance. Before Nvidia's earnings call this week, Ben Reitzes, a top tech analyst at Melius Research, laid out what interim leadership needs to do to steady the ship following Jensen Huang's ouster. At the top of his list was keeping Nvidia's engineers from leaving. "What's the go-forward plan there of retaining all the engineers?" Reitzes told investors in a video. "The road map, in our opinion, is actually the most important for a long-term investor. Can they keep it on track? What are they doing to retain the talent to keep it on track?" It's a crucial question for Nvidia, which has lost about $500 billion in market value since its board ousted Huang last week, sparking an extraordinary backlash from some employees, investors, and other technology leaders. Nvidia risks losing some of the engineers responsible for creating the chips and other highly technical systems that have made it the world's dominant AI hardware company. Technical talent is especially important in Silicon Valley because the products companies sell can change dramatically from one generation to the next. Compare that to a bank. Its core business involves accepting deposits, making loans, and managing investments. While leadership matters, the products are well established, and experienced executives can generally take over without having to reinvent them. Technology companies face a different challenge. Their success often depends on developing products that don't yet exist, anticipating what customers will need years in advance, and making technical decisions that competitors struggle to replicate. One mistake and a new wave of invention can wipe you out. That requires more than good management. It takes engineers with unusual skills, working under leaders who understand the technology well enough to recognize which ideas are worth pursuing — years before they materialize.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Huang combined those qualities at Nvidia. He helped turn a maker of graphics chips for video games into the company supplying much of the computing power behind the AI boom. His ouster raises questions about whether Nvidia can preserve that combination of technical expertise, leadership, and long-term vision. "A concentrated product brings concentrated risk," Christopher Brown, an investment professional at Synovus, told Business Insider. Nvidia is especially dependent on a closely connected collection of chips, software, and other technology that powers its AI business. Losing the people responsible for developing those products could therefore have an outsize impact, Brown said. Brad Gastwirth, head of research at Circular Technology, said the departure of just a handful of senior engineers could cause serious problems. "Losing even five to 10 critical technical leaders could have a disproportionate impact, particularly if those individuals are responsible for architectural decisions or coordinating major product transitions," he told Business Insider. Nvidia's competitors have plenty of reasons to take advantage of the turmoil. "I would absolutely expect competitors, including AMD, Broadcom, hyperscalers and AI startups, to aggressively recruit Nvidia engineers," Gastwirth said. Brown agreed, describing efforts to recruit Nvidia technical talent as inevitable. "His team loves him. And many of them are there because of him, and have had higher offers to go elsewhere and have turned them down because of personal loyalty to Jensen," Elon Musk said following Huang's departure. On Tuesday, Huang said he'd be honored to return as CEO if the board approves. He cited support from a wide range of constituents, and at the top of his list were Nvidia employees. "I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a statement. Thousands of Nvidia employees have signed an open letter calling for Huang's reinstatement, while some have publicly criticized the decision to oust him. "I'm deeply disappointed in our board," Nvidia research scientist Shang-Wen Li wrote on X on Wednesday. Darrell Dai, a Nvidia robotics researcher who resigned following Huang's ouster, praised the former CEO's willingness to invest in technologies before their commercial potential became obvious. Dai also highlighted the working environment Huang created. "Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes," he wrote. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, is trying to address the retention threat. At an Nvidia all-hands meeting Wednesday, Kress told employees that pay raises and additional stock grants would arrive in December, earlier than originally planned. The company also sought to reassure staff that its technology plans and relationships with customers remained intact. Even though Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, is widely respected on Wall Street, her background lacks the technical experience essential to shaping Nvidia's products over the next decade. The board is searching for a permanent CEO replacement, considering both internal and external candidates. In the meantime, money could help Nvidia retain engineers. One employee who attended Wednesday's all-hands meeting told Business Insider that better compensation is an attractive short-term incentive. The person questioned whether it would be enough over the longer term. They said that with the stock having already exploded over the past decade, the added compensation may not be a sufficient motivation. Indeed, Nvidia's extraordinary stock performance has already made many longtime employees millionaires, giving some considerable financial freedom. Gastwirth said the greater danger lies in what happens over the next several years, as Nvidia must make decisions about future generations of AI technology without the leader who helped establish its dominance. "Jensen wasn't simply managing Nvidia," he said. "He had an extraordinary ability to anticipate where computing and AI were heading and position the company years ahead of competitors." His departure could set off a chain reaction if other important technical leaders decide to leave, Gastwirth warned. "Nvidia could lose not only critical engineering expertise but also some of the strategic thinking that has allowed it to consistently stay ahead of the industry," he said. Have a tip? Ruby2Shell is a one-byte heap overflow to remote code execution in Ruby's string case conversion.           Reachable without authentication in the default configuration of           common Ruby web frameworks and self-hosted software.   The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.   These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come               from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed               release yet: every current version is vulnerable.   Updated 20 November 2026 at 04:59 UTC.   Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.   Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions               of popular products.   Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but               the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).   The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20               bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an               input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.   The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings               and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.   UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.   Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.   A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly               after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the               buffer through the input length.   Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of               bounds.   We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code               execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then.   Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the               first to demonstrate remote code execution.   The Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting               the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.  Resources Company © 2026 Veria Labs, Inc.

Lahori Zeera will close this year with $115-120m in revenue  It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment. Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients. They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially. Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour. The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin. Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; Â£0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m. Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.  Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.  There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.  Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company. "Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years." Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.  Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012. Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.  Cumin is a warm, earthy spice widely used in Indian cuisine  The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033. According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of  Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%. "This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016. "In global markets,â¯establishedâ¯duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; anâ¯8% swingâ¯in less than a year is a structural disruption." Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand". For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume. With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal. But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind. Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.  Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks. Global giants like Coca-Cola and Pepsi have long held a monopoly on India's carbonated beverages market  This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth. "The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC. The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword. While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.  Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.  Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category. "Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements. Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.  But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.  "Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years. "For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India." Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion). The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology. Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI. Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it? In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17. Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%. The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies. The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. "Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect." Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever. The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly. It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude. As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot. The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year. That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion. Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since. Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time. But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world. With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market. "There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said. Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? Daniela Amodei: Anthropic and the price of AI So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available. "We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows." A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term. One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached. Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.  Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."    The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations. A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible. Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously. Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product". "AI carries real risks," she added. Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history. AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut. Save Share Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June. The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each. The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts. Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece. The Claude creator is also set to raise $26bn through a private placement, a type of deal involving the sale of stock to private investors, taking the total capital raised to $107.3bn. SpaceX’s total IPO haul later came to $85.7bn, after the deal’s underwriters exercised an overallotment option to purchase additional shares. The blockbuster offering gives Anthropic a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, making it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla. Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”. The public listing of Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the AI rollout. Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI, anticipating it will usher in revolutionary changes in business and society. AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner. Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index. The spending frenzy has stoked debate over whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble like the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash. Anthropic’s listing also comes as the market for the advanced graphics processing units that power AI is under a cloud amid the spying claims roiling chip giant Nvidia. Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid unproven claims that a woman he was romantically involved with worked with the Chinese intelligence services. The scandal has fuelled calls in the United States for stronger restrictions on China’s access to high-end chips, casting a pall over an AI boom partly sustained by Chinese developers’ remote access to data centres in Southeast Asia. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index has shed 7.6 percent of its value over the past month, led by a more than 30 percent plunge in Nvidia’s stock price. Asian stock markets with heavy exposure to AI had a mixed session on Thursday amid the flurry of excitement around Anthropic. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 percent, while South Korea’s Kospi closed up 0.9 percent after sliding in morning trading. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index and Taiwan’s Taiex both finished in the red, shedding 2 percent and 4.4 percent, respectively. Nasdaq futures gained 1.9 percent ahead of Wall Street’s reopening. Jay R Ritter, an IPO expert at the University of Florida, said that Anthropic’s ability to make profits to justify its valuation will depend on various factors, some of which are outside its control. “Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives,” Ritter told Al Jazeera. “Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing. It will change our lives, too.” Ritter said investors are particularly excited about the potential of Anthropic’s AI models to find cures for conditions such as cancer and dementia in the near future. “When Google went public in 2004, no one knew whether it would be able to dominate on-line searches, and no one knew how lucrative the targeted search advertising business would become,” he said. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Anthropic’s strong debut should help reassure investors that the AI boom is sustainable. “At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Ives said in a note to clients. “It is going through a very turbulent, white-knuckle period that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years on the AI revolution,” Ives said, adding that Anthropic would be “a central player” in the buildout. Anthropic immediately became one of the largest public companies in the world. Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at a price of $111.50 a share, though the price dropped to $97.17 a share by the close of trading. Still, the company behind popular chatbot Claude occupied rarefied air among some of the largest public companies in the world. Anthropic's stock closed well above an offer price of $83 a share, which had valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. Dan Ives, a stock analyst at Yorkville Ives who focuses on tech, said on Thursday the stock debut provided a gauge of investor appetite for frontier AI models of the type made by Anthropic. Those models, in turn, fuel many AI products. "The AI revolution gets its public scoreboard," Ives said of Anthropic's stock listing. Even as Anthropic rose above its IPO price on Thursday, the broad stock indexes tumbled. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 1,100 points, or 2.1% while S&P 500 dropped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 2.2%. The drop in overall markets owed in part to an uptick in demand for Anthropic, which prompted some investors to sell shares in other firms, Mohammed El-Erian, former CEO and co-CIO of investment management firm PIMCO, said on social media. "Remember this isn't just about the promise of AI, but about making room for it," El-Erian said on X. "In a narrow sense, investor financing of the mega-IPO involves making room by selling other holdings." The Anthropic IPO arrived at a tumultuous moment for the AI industry. Public concern over potential catastrophic risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company. Nvidia, a high-flying AI firm and a partner of Anthropic, suffered a leadership shakeup last week as CEO Jensen Huang stepped down over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down about 4% since Huang resigned. Huang admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife," though he did not name the person with whom he had been involved. Here's what to know about the Anthropic IPO: The IPO pulled in fresh funds for the San Francisco-based firm, which aims to compete in a potentially lucrative but cost-intensive section of the AI industry centered on advanced models and the tools they empower. "Building and scaling frontier intelligence is one of the most important and capital-intensive endeavors in history," Anthropic said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Anthropic priced its initial public offering of 980 million shares at $83 a share -- raising $81 billion. Anthropic traded under the ticker symbol "ANT." The company significantly expanded its revenue at the outset of 2026, but it continued to suffer losses. Anthropic earned $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of this year, growing nearly 14-fold from the same period a year earlier, according to a government filing. Still, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion over the first six months of this year, indicating the scale of its spending over that period. Anthropic boasts seven co-founders, and each of them was expected to become a multi-billionaire after the company went public. The most well-known co-founder is CEO Dario Amodei, who has drawn attention for repeated warnings about the risks posed by AI. The company's other founders are Daniela Amodei, the company's chair, president and Dario's sister; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer; Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead. The founders each hold a stake of 3.6% to 3.7% of the company's voting common shares, and they each planned to sell a small portion of their stake when the company went public, according to a financial filing. At the previously anticipated share price of $70 to $78, the portion of the stake to be sold by each one would have amounted to about $250 million. The remaining stake held by each -- about 3.2% -- would have been valued at more than $17 billion. Anthropic will all but certainly become a part of people's 401(k) accounts soon. Those accounts often hold index funds, which are pegged to major indexes like the Nasdaq. Until recently, newly listed companies were barred from major indexes until after an extended waiting period. But the Nasdaq issued a rule change in May permitting "fast entry" to the Nasdaq-100 for some major IPOs. Over the ensuing weeks, some other top exchanges also tweaked their rules, though their eligibility requirements vary. "Although Anthropic is unlikely to join the S&P 500 before late 2027 because of eligibility requirements, it is expected to be added to other indexes relatively soon after listing," Brian Therien, senior analyst at Edward Jones, told ABC News in a statement. As such, it won't take long for Anthropic to become a part of 401(k) holdings. In the run-up to its IPO, Anthropic touted AI as a transformational and lucrative technology, while warning about possible catastrophic risk that could bring financial fallout for shareholders. A financial filing last month presents AI as "one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort." In the same document, Anthropic warned of the possibility its AI models could pose a "catastrophic or existential risk to humanity." Investing in the company's stock "involves a high degree of risk," Anthropic added. In a report ahead of the IPO, financial research firm Morningstar voiced optimism about the stock but also cautioned about a very high degree of uncertainty surrounding the firm's prospects. "We have a positive outlook on Anthropic's ability to remain at the frontier of artificial intelligence model research," Morningstar said, adding that the company could monetize such research by "selling primarily to enterprise customers." Still, Morningstar said its warning about uncertainty "reflects our view on the wide range of financial outcomes for a business investing heavily in large language models, a nascent technology." 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

"If you've got a whole family in the car, you still need autonomous vehicles for that, so what we plan to do is have an autonomous version of Model Y that wouldn't have steering wheels and pedals and would be good for transporting groups of six or seven people," Musk said. Tesla Robotaxi already uses Model Ys in its autonomous vehicle fleet, but it can transport only up to four passengers. A robotaxi capable of carrying six or seven passengers would give Tesla a way to serve larger groups, a segment of the US autonomous ride-hailing market that remains relatively underserved. Waymo's Ojai, which is supposed to be the company's more spacious vehicle platform compared to the Jaguar SUVs, can fit up to four people. Tech iFixit found the HomeView nearly impossible to repair yourself, but smart displays don't face the same daily risks as iPhones. Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home  				Edited by Gael Cooper  November 19, 2026, 4:22 am ET For the past few years, Apple was looking almost DIY-friendly. The company had been moving toward smart speakers that you could take apart without damaging and iPads with accessible batteries. But the new HomeView smart display broke apart when iFixit tried to access components in Tuesday’s full analysis. The good news? I don’t think it really matters, at least not for this particular Apple device. Here’s why.  DIY repairs are a big deal for Apple products, not just because they’re difficult, but because many people believe they have a right to repair their own phones or computers. More from CNET Making repairs more accessible also sustains a secondary market of iPhone and Mac repair services that Apple would rather tightly control — or squash entirely. That’s one reason the EU has required Apple to make iPhone batteries replaceable in 2027. The HomeView moves sharply in the opposite direction, held together by the toughest adhesive iFixit has ever encountered in an Apple product. The glue is so stubborn that the team accidentally snapped a speaker in half during disassembly, and the logic board was bound too dangerously tight to the aluminum chassis to remove. “Obviously, when you buy a product you don’t anticipate the accidents, and there’s no way of knowing when wear and tear will become a problem,” iFixit said in its report. “But you can be sure of one thing: The HomeView will not be an easy or pleasant repair when that time comes.” A representative from Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. iFixit also pointed out that if a HomeView device falls out of warranty, the repair typically costs as much as the $299 smart display itself. I’m just not sure any potential HomeView users need to worry about the device’s repairability the way they would about an iPhone or Mac. Smart displays don’t have the same DIY repair needs as the phone in your pocket. There’s no battery to replace, which is one of the most common reasons to open up an iPhone or MacBook. And while a shattered iPhone screen can easily be swapped out for a third-party replacement, no aftermarket alternatives exist for the HomeView’s custom 7-inch display. Since you can only get a replacement screen through Apple anyway, making the device easier to open wouldn’t actually help you fix it yourself. Plus, smart displays don’t face the same environmental risks as phones and laptops, which are constantly on the move, encounter dust in pockets, accidentally dropped and exposed to potential heat and rain. The HomeView is designed to remain stationary in your home. The need for DIY repairs is simply far less of a concern. I don’t mean to say iFixit’s teardown was unnecessary. We learned valuable information, including how the speakers and their connectors broke in several ways when iFixit tried to remove them. (The speaker assembly is actually one HomeView component I worry people may need to replace.) “Embedded speakers are a relatively common source of failure. The under-screen speakers inside the HomeView in particular, more closely resemble laptop speakers than HomePod tweeters,” the iFixit report notes. “As far as laptop and MacBook speakers go, we’ve seen plenty of examples of damage caused by accidents and wear and tear.” I’ve been testing smart displays and smart speakers since they first hit the market, and none of the devices I’ve tested have developed a blown or faulty speaker. In the HomePod subreddit, I couldn’t find any reports of speaker failures except from people already Frankensteining their Apple speakers with third-party components. I wouldn’t let the fear of repair difficulties get in the way of buying a HomeView. A bigger concern is the HomeView’s compact 7-inch screen, which feels cramped for watching video, especially compared with the larger displays Amazon has rolled out across its Echo Show lineup.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. When Jacob Coxon left Anthropic in September, his worries about AI development fueled nationwide fear about the tech. On Thursday, as the public got its hands on Anthropic stock for the first time, the researcher tried to bring people's attention back to the issue of safety. "It literally doesn't matter whether they invest," Coxon told Business Insider. "We have to stop RSI." RSI refers to recursive self-improvement, the tactic of getting advanced AI systems to train the next generations of AI. Coxon gathered with dozens of other people outside Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters for a "Ban RSI" protest on Thursday. The company's blockbuster initial public offering valued it at $1.7 trillion. Protesters chanted, lifted signs, and listened to speeches by Coxon, ex-OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, and YouTuber Rob Miles. A group of protesters from the organization Stop AI, who arrived later, blocked the office's entrance. An independent report from the AI safety organization METR recently found that AI use is already accelerating Anthropic's research and development efforts. Anthropic also wrote in its IPO prospectus that it doesn't expect that letting AI fully design its next generation without supervision would be safe. It wrote that it's considering policy updates, "to keep humans in control of frontier model development." Coxon says he would like to see more. He said in his speech that Anthropic should lobby the government and coordinate with other companies to secure a full ban on RSI. "At this point, the companies are the problem," he said. "There are only a few places in the world where recursive self-improvement is possible in 2027. And this office is one of them." Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. Coxon and Kokotajlo each spoke about how, in private, they hear AI researchers express alarm about the technology's risks. The concerns have reached Congress as well, where representatives have begun suggesting restrictions on RSI.
