One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence. Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza. In the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West. According to a rapid analysis that month by media researchers at the University of Washington, those 400 posts racked up an astonishing 370 million views. As the UW researchers framed it, a 641,000-follower Polish account had just catapulted itself atop a list of “new elites” on X, momentarily trouncing the reach of legacy outlets with follower counts in the tens of millions, like CNN, The New York Times, and the BBC. More to the point, Visegrad had also established itself overnight as one of the most influential pro-Israel accounts on X. And that’s what seemed to be giving Tompson pause. “With the Israel situation,” Tompson texted his colleague, “I do loathe Hamas, and it’s been the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west” (a long-standing editorial priority for Tompson and his team). But Tompson seemed wary that Israel was already angling for a wider regional conflict. “Personally I want that war to be contained where it is,” Tompson wrote. “And the Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things.” Ultimately, the founder reasoned a way through his qualms. In another message from the same day, the cigar-smoking, cravat-wearing, thirtysomething Tompson wrote to the same confidant—whom I’ll call Boris—to spell out how he’d landed with regard to V24’s “editorial line” on Israel. As Tompson saw it, V24 had been faced with “four options” once the war started: 1. Say nothing;2. Be objective—get hated by both sides;3. Pro Muslim—there are 1.5 billion of them;4. Pro Israel—There are fewer but also they have a lot of influence and money. In choosing between those options, Tompson laid out a blunt motivation: “My goal is to fundraise off of this,” he wrote. Covering Gaza did fit nicely with V24’s long-standing brand of anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, Western-chauvinist content. (“The beauty of this war is that it allows us to criticize slims—especially those in Europe—without any consequences,” Tompson would later write, using a shorthand slur for Muslims.) But now he seemed to have his eyes on a bigger opportunity: using Visegrad’s “new elite” status to rake in money from some of Israel’s most powerful supporters in Silicon Valley and beyond. And according to an extensive trove of V24 financial records, internal communications, screenshots from group chats, and correspondence with donors, all reviewed by WIRED, Tompson promptly succeeded at exactly that. Over the past six years, Visegrad24 has become a strangely ubiquitous force in right-wing social media, its feed a reliable kaleidoscope of dehumanized, brown-skinned aggressors and their alleged depredations against innocent, often white-skinned victims, alongside global news from a nationalist perspective. On any given day, V24 might show you a stomach-turning video of a camel being abused at a wedding in the West Bank, a parade of cell phone clips showing violent crimes being committed by alleged “migrants” all across Europe, or an interview about the Great Replacement Theory. From its headquarters in Warsaw, V24’s lean pseudo-news operation has proven itself almost preternaturally adept at virality on Elon Musk’s X. It even seems to have become one of the oligarch’s own favorite accounts. For a period after November 2024, Musk became especially fixated on British far-right politics, posting nonstop about “rape gangs” of South Asian men allegedly grooming British girls. To better understand Musk’s influences at the time, WIRED partnered with the research firm Bright Data to analyze his interactions with some 30 prominent European far-right accounts over a 45-day period ending in January 2025; we found that Musk engaged with Visegrad24, a major font of “grooming gangs” content, at least three times more than any other account on the list. Another dubious mark of distinction for V24: Of all the billion-plus accounts on X, Visegrad ranks 32nd in the number of community notes—crowdsourced fact checks—that have been attached to its posts. But in tandem with its drumbeat of demonized migrants, V24 has also excelled at capitalizing on the information wars that inevitably form around real, bloody conflicts like those in Ukraine, Gaza, and now Iran. The documents obtained by WIRED—to which Tompson responded with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer—shed an intimate light on how this playbook evolved over the course of V24’s rapid rise. They provide an unvarnished case study of life inside today’s fractured and erratic right-wing mediasphere. And they reveal how the right kind of online influence, even when it’s strategically acquired by an entity just barely above the gutter of white nationalism, can command support from some of the most powerful people in the world. In late November 2023, Tompson wrote to Boris with some exciting news. “Jewish VCs have created a group,” he texted. “Several. I’m in two of those groups that actively push back against founders who have supported Palestine.” In another message he described one of these encrypted text threads as “85 people. 84 Jews and me.” “They are slowly reaching out directly … Usually they want a retweet,” he wrote to Boris. “V24 is such a big part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now.” “You’re in the belly of the beast now,” replied Boris (who requested anonymity for fear of legal retaliation). One of the groups to which Tompson gained entry was called Jewish Alliances, described by one of its members—someone going by the handle Sean Rad, which is the name of a Tinder cofounder—as a space to “bring together Jews and non-Jews working together to fight antisemitism.” On Jewish Alliances, Tompson came personally recommended by Shaun Maguire, a general partner at Sequoia Capital who led the firm’s investments in Elon Musk–affiliated companies. Like V24, Maguire had become vociferously pro-Israel after October 7—later explaining that the attacks galvanized him to engage in “information warfare” for the country. Maguire had even made introductions that eventually helped connect the Israel Defense Forces with Musk’s Starlink satellite communication network in the earliest days of the Gaza war. And now, on Jewish Alliances, he was throwing some weight behind V24. “Stefan / Visegrad is an incredible account if you’re not already following,” Maguire told the group thread. Privately, Maguire told Tompson, “I’ll give u $25k and try to raise the rest.” (Maguire later told WIRED that he ultimately had to stop short of making his donation. “I would have loved to donate to Visegrad, as I think their content is excellent, but I wasn't able to for compliance reasons.”) As for the other elite group chat that Tompson says he was invited to join, it appears to have been even more rarefied. In December that year, Tompson sent Boris a screenshot of a blurb from a Puck newsletter, headlined “The In-Crowd’s Hottest Text Thread.” Tompson had circled the item in red with an arrow pointing at it. “I learned this week that hundreds of the most powerful figures from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Hollywood have joined a sprawling, informal WhatsApp thread to share thoughts on how to build support for Israel and combat antisemitism following the attacks of October 7,” wrote media reporter Dylan Byers in the blurb. “The group, which is called Builders for Israel, includes the likes of Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, and David Marcus.” “And Stefan Tompson 😂,” Boris replied, to which Tompson responded with his own laughing emoji. On the two group chats, Tompson sometimes gawked at the proceedings, sending Boris screenshots of what he was witnessing. On November 24, one member posted the following message to the group: “I bought some domains. If anyone would like them to redirect to appropriate content lmk.” The member then listed out a series of five urls: “longlivetheintifada.com, wechargeyouwithgenocide.com, palestineisourhome.com, fromtherivertothesee.com, fromtheriver2theseapalestinewillbefree.com.” “Btw this is available albeit $75k,” the member went on, before posting a screenshot showing a listing for the domain name “Allahuakbar.com.” Tompson himself responded inside the group. “Oh this has so much potential! 💀” he wrote. (A review of public web domain records shows that all five of the first urls listed here were registered through GoDaddy using Domains by Proxy, a service that allows domain registrants to hide their personal contact information. The records show that all five were created on November 22, 2023, in two batches 33 minutes apart.  It’s unclear whether anyone bought Allahuakbar.com, whose owner is also hidden behind the proxy service, but its registration record was last updated on November 28, 2023.) As a platform for fundraising, the two group chats appear to have paid off pretty handsomely for Visegrad24. “Should have 75k on Monday,” Tompson wrote to Boris on November 18. There was $50,000 coming from “a very private man” at the Silicon Valley fintech investment firm Ribbit Capital. Ribbit's founder is Meyer “Micky” Malka, an early investor in Coinbase and promoter of crypto. Tompson would later tell Boris that Malka was allegedly planning to donate an additional $200,000. Financial records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 roughly lining up with Tompson's messages, but Malka did not respond to requests for comment. Records indicate that Tompson also secured a $20,000 donation from the investment firm Hindenberg Research, with an additional $15,000 linked to an email address associated with the firm’s founder, the prominent Wall Street short seller Nathan Anderson. Tompson also claimed he had a “soft commitment” from the Israeli American investor Daniel Gross, a former AI lead at both Apple and Y Combinator. (Anderson did not respond to requests for comment; Gross’s representatives said they have no record of a donation.) Notifications from GiveButter, a site Tompson used for soliciting contributions, show that other donations were linked to email addresses associated with SimpleVenue CEO Michael Sinensky, Warby Parker founder Neil Blumenthal, Wix president Nir Zohar, Lux Capital cofounder Josh Wolfe, and deep tech venture capitalist Matt Ocko. (Sinensky and Blumenthal declined to comment, and Zohar’s representatives said they had no record of him donating. Wolfe and Ocko neither confirmed nor denied that they’d given money to V24, but both came back with remarkably similar responses, primarily taking issue with WIRED’s characterization of whether Visegrad is “far right.” “I don't fund or support ‘far right’ groups,” Wolfe wrote, “and thankfully Stefan and Visegard24 are pro-democracy, pro-Western values, pro-peace and prosperity.” Wrote Ocko: “Even cursory research indicates that neither Mr. Tompson, nor Visegrad24 are affiliated with or support anything other than: classical liberal Western values, including the rule of law; the defense of democratic polities from terror and autocracies … peace and prosperity for all law-abiding and civilized people; opposition to horrific antisemitism and terrorist exaltation.”) While Tompson was fundraising away with his group-chat contacts, Boris wrote with a question. “By the way, should I take Middle Eastern money?” he asked, mentioning opportunities to raise funds from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. “100 percent yes. Play both sides,” Tompson said. “I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs.” To receive its donations, V24 set up an organization under the 501(c)(3) umbrella called the Intermarium Foundation, headquartered in Pennsylvania but domiciled in Delaware. Over the next year and more, over a million dollars poured in. Much of the money, including some of the largest sums, appears to have come in through “donor advised funds”—“dark money” philanthropic vehicles that allow donors to hide their identities, even from the recipients of their cash. Foundation documents show that in November 2024, the organization received $175,000 from DonorsTrust, a fund closely aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, often referred to as the “dark money ATM” of the American right. Documents also suggest that V24 received $172,000 from the Giving Back Fund, which describes itself as a “national nonprofit organization that encourages and facilitates charitable giving by professional athletes, celebrities, high-net-worth individuals, existing nonprofit organizations, corporations, and others.” A London-born self-described “Polish South African” who was “educated in French schools,” Tompson founded Visegrad24 in early 2020. He'd moved to Warsaw from London in the mid-2010s, having worked as a PR strategist on the “Leave” side of the Brexit campaign, according to Gizmodo. Tompson’s great-grandfather, he has said, was the Polish ambassador to England at the time of the Nazi invasion. Between the war and the communist takeover of Poland, the family was left stranded abroad for three generations. In a 2024 interview with Jewish Insider, Tompson referred to his arrival in Warsaw as his “own version of aliyah,” the Hebrew word used to describe a Jewish person’s immigration to Israel. Tompson’s homecoming took place just as Poland was attempting to aggressively pattern itself after Viktor Orban’s Hungary. In 2015, the illiberal, nationalist Law and Justice Party swept Polish elections and set about packing courts, hollowing institutions, and seizing control of Polish state radio, newspapers, and television—turning the latter into nakedly xenophobic, anti-opposition, and often antisemitic propaganda organs. With his taste for cravats and posh Barbour jackets, Tompson found an audience on Polish state TV documentaries extolling the country’s grand cultural heritage. He started a PR agency called Bracia Tompson SC, and according to the investigative site VSquare, he made short films with the support of something called the Institute for the Legacy of Polish National Thought, described by the Polish news outlet Polytka as a slush fund for the governing party. Tompson also spent the late 2010s working on what he described as a “three-hour documentary” about his father’s ancestral home, South Africa—a country whose quality of life, Tompson claimed in a 2019 Polish radio interview, is worse today than under apartheid. The documentary project was reportedly titled African Volhynia, after an area in Central Europe where Poles suffered historic massacres, land dispossession, and ethnic cleansing—a framing that, to some observers, strongly suggests that Tompson was packaging a South African “white genocide” narrative for a Polish audience. The full documentary, however, was never released. Instead, Tompson shifted focus to launch Visegrad24 in January 2020, with a logo closely mirroring the South African outlet News24. The name Visegrad is a reference to the Visegrad Group, an informal diplomatic bloc of four Central European nations that includes Poland and Hungary. In 2020, it was Poland’s turn to occupy the rotating presidency of the alliance—and V24 appears to have served a promotional function. When V24’s Facebook page was briefly blocked for violating community standards in 2021, the Polish deputy minister of foreign affairs spoke up for the account. “The Visegrad24 profile is not an official profile of the Visegrad Group or the Polish presidency of the Visegrad Group,” he told a Polish radio station. “However, we appreciate it for its promotion of the group’s activities.” One of Tompson’s main partners in the enterprise was a Polish journalist named Adam Starzynski, the former proprietor of an ultra-right-wing Twitter account called @BasedPoland and reportedly a fellow board member at something called the State of Poland Foundation. Their third, more silent founder was Tompson’s brother Jan. Tompson’s sister Alexandra also became involved, sometimes serving as a de facto legal rep. In its early years, Visegrad24 posted roughly in line with the Law and Justice Party’s priorities—positively about Poland’s abortion ban, negatively about migrants, fulsomely about Christianity and Hungarian fertility rates—and was tagged frequently by party officials, according to Polish investigative site OKO.Press. But Tompson harbored bigger ambitions, as well as some apparent personal struggles. In early 2022, Visegrad’s core team escaped the Polish winter by renting a house together in the Canary Islands—during which time Tompson was said to be “undergoing acute drug withdrawal and was in a very vulnerable state,” according to an email later written by Alexandra and reviewed by WIRED. (In a couple of messages, Tompson refers to a time in his life when he was “on coke.”) The team had been in Gran Canaria for about a month when something momentous happened: Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. In the early morning hours of February 24, they woke up to images of Russian tanks crossing Ukraine’s borders. They immediately began pushing out an intense volume of news and clickbait. Bit by bit, Visegrad started gaining international traction—and international notoriety for spreading fake news. On February 25, Visegrad tweeted “PornHub cockblocks Russian users,” alleging that Russian porn seekers “were presented with a message saying the content is blocked along with a Ukrainian flag and a message of support to Ukraine”—a rumor that was debunked by Snopes and other online fact-checkers. Then, about a week later, V24 tweeted that actor Leonardo DiCaprio had donated $10 million to Ukraine in honor of his grandmother from Odesa. (DiCaprio made no such donation, and there is no evidence of such a grandmother.) Articles debunking V24’s claim promptly appeared on Snopes and CNN. This first brush with global virality came with risks. Elon Musk didn’t own Twitter yet, and content moderation was strict. “I’m really stressing out over v24,” Tompson wrote in an internal WhatsApp group named Gran Canaria. But rather than get shut down, V24 lived to see its follower count triple, growing from 80,000 to 250,000 in weeks. V24’s boosted reach didn’t bring an end to Tompson’s frustrations, however. He appeared dissatisfied with the liberal followers that came along with being such a prominent pro-Ukrainian account. And he also seemed to be running into patronage problems: In 2022, the Polish news outlet Wiadomości revealed that the office of Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had tried to allocate about $300,000 for “the implementation of the public project titled ‘Visegrad24,’” sending money to a sports and fitness NGO called the Action-Life Foundation. Then, in 2023, according to OKO.press, Morawiecki’s office appears to have sent a bit under $600,000 for a “media center” at the Action-Life Foundation—which appeared, yet again, to be a carve-out for a V24-affiliated project. This time the grant was recalled after public outcry. (In an interview, Tompson has said he “never had a penny to run Visegrad” from the Polish state.) In October 2023, the Law & Justice Party lost its majority in parliament, ending eight years of right-wing dominance over Polish government purse strings. By that fall, Tompson seems to have realized that V24’s Canary Islands posting blitz had yielded a huge bump in influence that they’d failed to monetize. In terms of fundraising, Tompson told Boris, “we missed the boat with Ukraine.” So when V24 repeated its flood-the-zone strategy with the October 7 attacks, Tompson seemed determined not to skip the next step. By early 2024, Tompson was sitting down in Tel Aviv for a podcast interview with the American-born Israeli venture capitalist Michael Eisenberg—often billed as an informal adviser to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Less than six months had passed since October 7, and Tompson was on his way to becoming a minor celebrity among friends of Israel. “Meet the Man Who Shapes Millions of Twitter Users’ view of Israel’s war,” ran the headline of a story in the Jewish Chronicle, which went on to describe a series of V24 videos Tompson’s team had been filming on the streets of the West Bank. “Anyone who says it is an apartheid state in Israel and the Palestinian people are subjugated should go to Ramallah,” Tompson told the news outlet. “There were Maseratis and Mercedes and a brand-new shopping mall.” As of that month, at least 28,473 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since October 7, and at least 388 had been killed in the West Bank, Israel, and East Jerusalem, according to the United Nations. Tompson was also busily fundraising. “The west is under attack,” claimed a sleek V24 donor pitch deck dated August 2024 and later reviewed by WIRED. “We face two major adversaries: radical progressives” and “nefarious States (Russia, Iran, China, Qatar).” The pitch deck called V24 “the frontier of modern journalism for western values.” One pitch deck promoted “Project Q,” a social media campaign against Qatar. In a single month, Project Q had delivered “97 posts about Qatar across multiple accounts,” 12 original pieces of video content, including a “viral” short featuring the British anti-Islamic activist Tommy Robinson, video essays, and an instance of then Polish MEP Michał Dworczyk condemning Qatar in a speech. V24 also boasted that it was building “a network of Muslim and Arab influencers to push content,” including pro-Israel voices Loay Alshareef, Nuseir Yassin, Luai Ahmed, and YouTuber “Apostate Prophet,” the latter an ex-Muslim interviewee on V24’s YouTube. Then there was the Project Veritas–style hidden-camera news operation Tompson had launched, called V24 Investigations, run by the ex-Project Veritas board member Matthew Tyrmand. In the spring of 2024, V24 Investigations fanned out across American university campuses amid pro-Palestine protests to make unflattering, Project Veritas–style videos of student activists, part of a larger V24 effort to expand its YouTube presence. In reality, many of Visegrad’s new ventures were struggling to gain traction. Even today, Visegrad24’s YouTube channel has a relatively modest 180,000 subscribers, despite its billing as “Europe’s Leading News Hub.” An August 2025 video called “24 Hours in East London’s Muslim Area” garnered 2 million views, and about 20 videos—including several featuring Tommy Robinson—have exceeded 100,000 views. Most have failed to crack 10,000. V24 Investigations has gone completely dormant. Posts on the spinoff account Middle East 24 frequently fail to surpass 10 likes on X. The same is true of the Spanish-language page Visegrad24ES, despite its billing as “the world’s most viral group.” But in 2025 and 2026, Visegrad would see more opportunity to draw on a traditional area of strength—breaking war news on X. On June 13, 2025, Israel leaped into the wider conflict that Tompson had initially been afraid of: That morning, Tel Aviv brutally ambushed Iran with an onslaught of synchronized assassinations, air raids, and drone strikes—and V24 aggressively posted through it on X. But this time, alongside its fairly typical mix of war porn and mockery of pro-Palestinian protesters, a somewhat unusual motif ran through Visegrad’s social coverage of the war: Enthusiasm for restoring the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah. V24 even played a bit part in the social media war to influence US president Donald Trump as he toyed with joining Israel’s fight. On the fifth day of the war—after Trump had stated on Truth Social, “We know exactly where the so-called ‘Supreme Leader’ is hiding”—Visegrad chimed in with a post on X seemingly tailor-made to sweeten the option of regime change: Incoming reports of Iranian military officers seeking contact with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi to declare their intent to defect. They also want to pledge their allegiance to His Majesty and his mission to lead the transition to democracy in Iran after the regime’s fall. Visegrad’s post received more than a million views and was shared nearly 3,000 times. When Trump finally did make his move four days later, dropping a set of “bunker buster” bombs on Iranian nuclear sites, V24 posted an image of the Islamic Republic’s flag being torn away to reveal that of the Pahlavi monarchy and the words “It’s time” (2.4 million views, 3,600 shares). Why the outsize focus on the sexagenarian exiled son of a former dictator? Pahlavi does enjoy a certain amount of organic political support among the Iranian diaspora. But he’s also been held up at times as Israel’s preferred leader for Iran. In October 2025, Haaretz, TheMarker, and the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab reported that Israel’s government was likely behind a massive Persian-language “influence operation” to simulate online support for Pahlavi using bots, synchronized posting campaigns, and artificial intelligence—all “as part of an even broader Israeli campaign to influence the social media discourse.” V24’s own pro-Pahlavi posting binge was underway at the same time. When asked whether V24 had received any funding from Pahlavi’s network, Tompson responded by saying, “I wasn’t aware that Reza Pahlavi was a foreign state.” When asked whether he had received any money from Israel directly, Tompson replied with an apparent joke. “Yes,” he wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu personally hands me money for every post on Visegrad24.” In the three years since October 7, Visegrad24’s follower count has swelled to 2.1 million on X. But even as Musk’s platform has stubbornly remained V24’s only real area of strength, it has also become a more contested one since 2023. “They’re operating in an extremely competitive space,” says Ryan Broderick, the founder of the Garbage Day newsletter, which tracks the online media ecosystem. In recent years, with the rise of open-source-intelligence “monitoring the situation” accounts on X—essentially breaking-news channels run by hyper-online finance people—real-time coverage of crises and conflicts has become more of a crowded market, says Broderick. Today, he figures, an October 7–style V24 posting blitz would have a harder time breaking through. At the same time, V24’s other stock and trade—xenophobic posts about migrants—is easily upstaged by countless accounts that are more nakedly, brazenly racist. Meanwhile, support for Israel has only become a more isolating position to occupy on the global far right, which has leaned further and further into its natural affinity for noxious antisemitism. (In 2025, Tompson appears to have met up in Turkey with another right-wing video creator named Lord Miles—a British self-styled adventurer who denigrates many of the same ethnic groups that V24 does, only with the addition of being blatantly antisemitic. According to Lord Miles, the two were set to collaborate on a video. But then Tompson started talking about raising six-figure sums from a pro-Israel “WhatsApp group chat,” and Lord Miles bolted from the scene, later posting about the episode on X.) Relatively early in its reporting on V24, WIRED reached out to some people who know Tompson, including an ex-partner. Shortly afterward, Tompson called back from her phone. “That’s not how we do things in South Africa, my friend,” he said. “I don’t like it. I find it creepy; I find it weird.” He then offered to pay for a flight to Warsaw for an on-the-record interview with him—an offer WIRED declined, given journalistic standards against accepting money from sources. “Are you not a man, my friend?” Tompson said. “I’m very upset you have disrespected me.” When WIRED later got in touch to arrange a concrete date for a phone interview, Tompson asked if he could be sent questions in advance. When WIRED refused, citing standard editorial practice, Tompson balked. “Not really interested in you wasting my time old sport,” he wrote, “What exactly is the incentive for me to give you any more of my time, generosity or politeness?” He signed off the message with the words, “praying that you find Christ, who redeems all, including the likes of sinning wretches like myself.” He later turned WIRED’s reporter’s request for an interview around. “Now I am kindly offering you the opportunity to answer some questions,” he wrote. “It’s a generous offer, which will allow you to give your perspective on things and answer some important questions about your behavior, your lifestyle, your funding, and some other details that are an important reflection of you who are as a person.” WIRED declined. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sean Owen, 37, a Michigan-based former supply chain professional who now co-owns a mold remediation company. It's been edited for length and clarity. I had a corporate career at large companies like Whirlpool and SpaceX. Then, a mold remediation side hustle grew from a little business I ran with a friend in his garage to a company operating in six different markets. I found that entrepreneurship in the blue-collar industry not only paid more, but I also preferred the lifestyle. I graduated from Brigham Young University in 2019 and got into supply chain early on. I joined Whirlpool right out of college, and was based in Southern Michigan in their global supply chain leadership development program for three years. I enjoyed it.  In 2023, I began working for SpaceX, at the Starbase location in southern Texas. There was so much going on at the company, and the job itself was very exciting and fulfilling. I loved it. The hours, however, were crazy; on a good day, I was getting home at 8 p.m. I also didn't have the best boss. Also, we lived just eight minutes from the border of Mexico, and soon after arriving there, we heard a news story about a car of Americans who crossed over the border and were kidnapped. With having a wife and kids, it didn't feel like the ideal location to raise a family. Due to those three factors, I realized the job wasn't what I wanted. Later that year, we moved back to Michigan, where a former coworker of mine from Whirlpool helped me get a job with his new employer, Colson. One day, my old coworker and I went out to lunch, and I complimented his Ford F-150 and told him I'd always wanted one.  That conversation opened the door to a discussion about me helping him with his mold remediation business he'd started earlier that year called Mold Warrior. He'd found success working on it on the side during nights and weekends to make some extra money. We continued to discuss the possibility of partnering on the business, and about a month later, in January 2024, we decided to officially do so. I didn't have any experience with mold remediation, but I'm a handy guy, and I took a training course to get up to speed. At first, we didn't have formal roles; we decided to figure out the business together and became close friends through the process. We kept it as a side hustle for a while and only did a handful of mold removal jobs. Then, we hired and trained a technician to help us, so we could continue our full-time jobs while handling logistics outside our regular working hours. We spent most of our time answering phones, doing inspections, building out quotes, communicating with clients, and branding the company. We'd spend about 20 to 30 hours a week on Mold Warrior, switching off doing inspections at night so we'd each only be away from our families two to three nights a week. We weren't about to go all in until we knew we could support our families. We had goals to reach a consistent revenue target for a few months in a row before we would leave our full-time jobs. Getting two large water damage jobs helped us put a safety net in our bank accounts that made going all-in feel safer. My wife was very supportive, especially once I started sharing the revenue numbers with her and she saw that my take-home pay would be more than I'd made at my full-time job. Before that, she just saw me talking on the phone with my friend at all hours of the day and would sometimes be kind of annoyed. Once she saw the business was legitimate, though, I was probably more nervous about jumping into it than she was. She was excited I was going to be home more often and would have more freedom. My parents and siblings never gave me a hard time or questioned my decisions. Behind the scenes, they were probably thinking, "What is he doing?" but they never voiced that. Today, I run the Michigan market. My friend runs the Columbus market, where he moved in 2024, and we have four franchises throughout the country. I've been working in the field three to four days a week, doing inspections one day a week, and then having a lighter day of admin work where I catch up on emails. Right now, most of our jobs are residential, but we've had a handful of commercial projects. We have four full-time employees: a customer service rep, a technician in Ohio, and two technicians in Michigan, where we're looking to hire a third to keep up with demand. We also have four part-time employees who work for us on an as-needed basis and hire high schoolers to help out part-time during the summer. Our corporate backgrounds have translated nicely into putting forth a professional face in the blue-collar industry. A lot of our customers are affluent, so having experience presenting to high-level leaders has helped us a lot in communicating with CEOs and other professionals. Now, I don't have to worry about things like how I'm wording an email. There's no office politics. I don't have to deal with a manager because I am the manager. I don't have to please anyone but my customers. I do miss the excitement of working at Starbase around their Starship test flights. I keep up to date on SpaceX and have watched each of the test flights since leaving. While I'm watching, I miss working there, but then I remember how much work it was and how late I'd get home, and I snap out of it quickly. Sometimes I feel that people treat me differently now that I work in a blue-collar industry, but I don't care. If anything, it motivates me to keep dialing in my business so I can work less and make more money. I get to make my own schedule, and I can work as much, or as little, as I want. I'm proud of the freedom I've created, which allows me to be with my family and help out my wife more with our four young kids. The goal is to make myself irrelevant — to keep growing it and creating a sellable company. Do you have a story to share about pivoting from a corporate job to a blue-collar job? Published September 17, 2026 • 11 min read • Forecasts and price data checked September 2026 Photo: Sandisk on Unsplash. It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output. That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch. We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end? While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record. NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash. Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly. Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records. Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers. The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this. The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns. Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways. SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too. Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall. TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026. At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter, with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND, and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay. Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027. New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down. Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024. You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history. That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027: DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises. For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop. Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead. Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached. Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices. Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction. Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed. Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once. It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices. It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers. That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it. Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices. A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how. SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall. Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased. The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged. If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices. Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut. TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop. Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast. If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect. AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking. Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts. The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. The US Army posted an urgent request last week seeking contractors to quickly build concrete bunkers to replace shipping-container shelters at military installations across the Middle East. The Army initially included supporting documents detailing each project and its tight construction timeline, but later removed them from the posting, the status of which has been in flux. The notice, posted on a federal contracting website, said the Army needed 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers installed at five sites in Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Lebanon. It said the bunkers would provide better protection against indirect fire, as well as missiles and drones, as US forces face continued dangers in the region. Amid conflicts in the Middle East, American troops in the region have faced the threat of drone and missile strikes while using "non-standard containerized shelters," the notice said. "Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters," the Army said in the notice before removing them. Business Insider reviewed the documents before their removal on Tuesday. The service said it was seeking companies capable of manufacturing and installing the bunkers on an unusually tight construction timeline. Contractors would have just 45 days to complete the work. The posted notice cited "extreme operational urgency," explaining that "soldiers currently at risk using non-standard containerized shelters" need better protection as soon as possible. The page has oscillated between canceled and inactive, but the Army says it is still interested in better force protection solutions. "To ensure administrative accuracy and adhere to standard procurement best practices, a routine administrative update was made to the market research notice," Col. Adam Hallmark, a spokesperson for US Army Central, told Business Insider, explaining that the project predates recent overseas operations. He added that "these force protection requirements remain entirely valid as we continue to support and safeguard our personnel across the area of responsibility." The posted request for new bunkers comes after Iranian missile and drone attacks put US personnel at sustained risk and exposed vulnerabilities at American military installations across the Middle East during the military's war against Iran. Earlier this year, Iranian attacks on US locations severely damaged military base infrastructure and equipment. Six service members died in an attack on a US base in Kuwait, underscoring the danger troops face from aerial attacks. There have been concerns since the start of the war about whether US forces were sufficiently protected structures that had become common during the post-9/11 wars — trailers and other unhardened facilities often surrounded by thick concrete barriers to defend against ground threats, like gunshots and improvised explosive devices. The bunkers the Army described in the notice are designed for rapid installation. Each consists of three prefabricated reinforced-concrete sections, with steel protective doors and heavy concrete barriers shielding the entrances. Author of the Legal AI Insider newsletter Erika Fisher once thought a corporate legal team could build much of its own technology. Then she saw how quickly that do-it-yourself attitude could turn lawyers into IT managers. Now, the former HubSpot legal chief is joining Legora, one of the startups she initially dismissed, as its first chief legal officer. Fisher will lead Legora's legal function and help shape what it builds next for corporate legal departments. It helps that she speaks their language. Before HubSpot, Fisher spent nearly a decade at Atlassian, where she rose through the ranks to become chief administrative and legal officer. Her hiring comes as the contest for corporate legal departments heats up. Legora started its life selling software to law firms. Sales exploded as lawyers came under pressure from clients to move faster with technology. In 18 months, the yearly value of Legora's subscription business snowballed from $1 million to $100 million. Then, Legora took its pitch to the lawyers working inside companies.  Those teams face a different set of pressures. In-house lawyers are expected to protect the business without slowing it down. A delay can mean a deal falls apart or a job candidate walks. Software that cuts a task from days to minutes, or helps keep work in-house, has obvious appeal. Legora is turning that demand into business. In-house legal teams accounted for only a small fraction of its customers a year ago. They made up more than 40% of new customers in the third quarter, and helped push annual recurring revenue past $200 million, the company said. Its corporate customers include Salesforce, Broadcom, and Palo Alto Networks. "She knows what lawyers need from technology to do more in their day," Max Junestrand, Legora's chief executive, said in a statement. '"She will make sure Legora keeps building for that." Legora is hardly alone in chasing this market. Its closest rival, Harvey, says it has locked up 20% of the Fortune 500 as customers. Fisher knows the competition well. HubSpot is a Harvey customer, and its chief executive, Brian Halligan, has served as an informal advisor to the startup. Meanwhile, a growing crop of startups, including Wordsmith and Sandstone, is building software specifically for in-house lawyers. The field is more crowded than in Big Law, where the choice often comes down to Harvey, Legora, or both. The competition is coming from another direction, too. Tech giants like Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are now tailoring their models to specialized work, much as they did for coders, and building tools that lawyers can use directly. That puts startups like Harvey and Legora in an uncomfortable position. Their model suppliers are increasingly becoming their competition. The danger is that customers start to see them as little more than token resellers. Fisher thinks the threat is overblown. At HubSpot, she saw how access to powerful models enabled her team to build almost anything. That didn't mean they should. The more tools they developed, the more time lawyers spent maintaining them rather than practicing law. She argues that Legora takes that work off the legal department's plate, freeing lawyers to tackle more consequential work. The startup is betting that's how it earns its keep, even as the model labs encroach on its turf. "I think we need everybody solving the very best things that they're best at for the customer," Fisher said. Jump to

If you're out of work and believe the outlook for a new job is too dreary, you're probably being overly pessimistic. That might sound like something your mother would say, but new data shows that, since the pandemic, newly-unemployed Americans aren't very good at assessing how easily they'll get rehired — especially younger workers. An analysis from the New York Federal Reserve's Liberty Street Economics blog looks at how workers' expectations of finding a new job stacked up against reality. Before 2020, Americans were pretty good at predicting their employment prospects; the expected job-finding rate and the actual job-finding rate tracked closely together, according to the authors' analysis of the Current Population Survey and the Survey of Consumer Expectations. It follows newly unemployed workers, who have been jobless and looking for four weeks or fewer, and their actual success at finding a new role. But when the pandemic hit, workers' expectations of how easy it is to find a job diverged from reality, and haven't come back in line. In other words, workers are far too pessimistic about their ability to find a job. That's being driven especially by younger workers under 30. Before the pandemic, younger workers actually felt overconfident about their ability to find a job, tracking above their actual results. But after the pandemic, that optimism soured drastically. Workers under 30 went from overstating their expected job-finding rates by 6.3 percentage points to understating them by 3 percentage points. That might stem from pandemic-era labor market scars; Gen Z workers were disproportionately laid off in the immediate onset of the pandemic, with 25% of workers ages 16 to 24 in 2020 losing their jobs. Now, when Gen Z loses a job, they're much more likely to think they won't land a new role — even though that's not the reality. It's not just younger workers feeling unduly shaky about their stability. Tenured workers — who were likely further ahead in their careers than that younger group — are still worried about losing their roles. The New York Fed analysis finds another mismatch there: Historically, the longer a worker stays in the job, the less likely they are to lose that job. But workers don't feel that way — after two years, the actual job loss rate is half of the perceived job loss rate. In other words, workers are much more likely to keep their jobs after spending time in those roles, but they don't feel that way. That may be yet another layoff scar shaping workers' perceptions of their own standings. It might also be driven by another recession-battered generation. By   	CT Jones   	In author Suzanne Collins’ dystopian YA novel The Hunger Games, a reluctant teen revolutionary named Katniss Everdeen destroys a fascist government that broadcasts children fighting to the death for sport. The book makes pointed critiques of the fictional Capitol’s ruling class, constantly juxtaposing government-created poverty, violence, and forced labor with a cadre of one percenters whose lives are focused on high fashion, merriment, and excess. It’s a moral lesson served on a platter for middle-grade readers: Look for the bad guys — they’re the ones in the sparkling ball gowns, fat and happy while the protagonists suffer.   	In the close to two decades since Collins published The Hunger Games in 2008, the now five-novel series has grown into a cultural phenomenon with 100 million books sold and a blockbuster film franchise. Out Nov. 20, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, based on the 2025 book of the same name, is the latest adaptation of Collins’ world to the screen — a prequel charting the heartbreaking life of Haymitch Abernathy before he was Katniss’ drunk mentor and friend. (Joseph Zada stars in Sunrise on the Reaping; in the original films, an older Haymitch is played by Woody Harrelson.) With new stars and the return of original cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Harrelson, Sunrise on the Reaping has been positioned as the dominant big-budget film of the Thanksgiving holiday, enjoying months of promotional stunts, lavish influencer parties, international installations, and couture-themed red carpets. It’s a blitz of glossy promotion for the sixth film in the franchise and the second in under three years. So why is it, after all this time, The Hunger Games franchise still hasn’t figured out that its marketing misses the entire point of its films?   	           	In Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch is chosen as one of District 12’s male tributes — sent with Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) to the Capitol to fight to the death in a deceptively pastoral arena. But while citizens of Panem revel in the mental games of sponsors, allies, and grievous bloodshed, Haymitch is drafted to be the linchpin of a secret District rebellion. If Katniss is a symbol later in the series, Haymitch is a blunt weapon in his standalone film — a devastating and tragic example that revolution often requires sacrifices from people who will never see the fruits of their labor. But you wouldn’t be able to tell that from Sunrise on the Reaping’s pre-release campaign.   	            	 		Editor’s picks 	 	            	 	 		 					The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far		 	               	 	 		 					The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					100 Best Movies of the 21st Century		 	         	For Paris’ October Fashion Week, the studio behind the film, Lionsgate, held a Sunrise on the Reaping-themed costume exhibition at the sculpture garden of the Musée Rodin, a two-day experience titled “Elegance Is Authority: The Story, Style and Power of Panem.” Cast from the film attended the opening, complete with a six-course dinner incorporating themes for each of the 12 Districts, according to WWD. Outside the film’s promotional bubble, social media timelines were splashed with a viral video of a French orchestra playing the Hunger Games rebellion theme, “The Hanging Tree,” outside during the ongoing French student protests. (They only stopped when they were teargassed by police.) Cosmetics brand Stila was chosen as the official partner for the film and launched an accompanying makeup collection, including a “Sunrise Eyes Liqua-Play” shadow collection with shades “Maysilee,” “Lenore Dove,” and “Mags” named after women murdered by the Capitol. At this week’s New York premiere, attendees were encouraged to follow a “Make Them Remember You” theme for their attire — advice Haymitch gives to Katniss in the first film in an effort to help her survive. According to Vogue, people dressed in Capitol-inspired party outfits walked over to the official afterparty at the tony Metropolitan Club, which had been decorated with ice sculptures and Panem flags. Everything from television spots to posters, cast interviews, and fan events for the film has had this emphasis on spectacle and excess — a focus that completely ignores the story’s inherent social critiques.       	 		Trending Stories 	 	       	 	 		 					John Mayer Transports Michael J. Fox Back to the Future With Chuck Berry Performance		 	          	 	 		 					Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis		 	          	 	 		 					CMA Awards 2026: The Complete Winners List		 	          	 	 		 					Halestorm, Brothers Osborne, Hardy Sing for Brooks & Dunn at Ferocious 2026 CMA Tribute		 	          	 		Related Content 	 	       	 	 		 					Hear Ella Langley’s Reflective ‘Hunger Games’ Single ‘Here Then We’re Gone’		 	          	 	 		 					New ‘Hunger Games’ Novel Coming in 2025 From Suzanne Collins		 	          	 	 		 					Where to Stream All the 'Hunger Games' Films Before You Watch 'Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes'		 	          	 	 		 					'The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes' Is One Stuffed (But Satisfying) Prequel		 	         Sunrise on the Reaping isn’t the only Hunger Games film that’s fallen into this trap. There’s a consistent pattern of tone-deaf or straight-up ridiculous promotional attempts across the franchise. In 2025, Lionsgate announced a Hunger Games merch collaboration with fast-fashion company Shein — which fans balked at, considering the books’ themes about child exploitation and labor rights stand in opposition to the clothing giant known for its brutal working conditions. In 2014, for Mockingjay — Part 1, the Hunger Games promotional team released a version of “The Hanging Tree” titled the “Rebel Remix” — EDM tones and synth added to make the dirge fit for radio play. “Are you, are you/Coming to the tree?” a sped-up version of Lawrence’s voice sings, calling for rebels to fight the Capitol and “Wear a necklace of hope/Side by side with me.” (Yeah, seems fun to dance to.) Perhaps the most notorious example happened in 2013, when makeup brand CoverGirl launched its Capitol Collection, inspired by the best and richest looks in Panem. The backlash was so immediate that it inspired one the most longstanding memes on Tumblr — a parody Katniss Everdeen makeup tutorial with the instructions “we’re going to use a black eyeshadow to represent the coal mines that her father was smashed to death in.”  	           	When Collins published A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020, her first Hunger Games book in a decade, she told her publisher she had returned to the story because she thought people were beginning to “lose sight” of the dangers of authoritarian rule and what it takes to slowly dismantle a democracy. It’s not a coincidence that younger generations are flocking back to dystopian stories — the ones publishers and studios alike were convinced were flagging — at the same time that they’re becoming more politically minded. Collins’ books and the films based on them present a fictionalized and desperate endpoint to totalitarian ideas; one that readers and moviegoers are treating as more important than ever. But in the promotion of these films, Hollywood not only misrepresents the message of its source material, but betrays a striking lack of faith in the rich world the series has built — and the viewers who believe in its power. Donate today  Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations A new City Council bill would ban idling diesel-powered refrigerated trailers in New York City warehouses, targeting a major polluter in the South Bronx: Hunts Point Produce Market. The measure, which will be introduced Thursday by City Councilmember Justin Sanchez of the Bronx, seeks to force an end to the trailers that have long been a symbol of the environmental injustice that helped the South Bronx earn the nickname “asthma alley.” Gothamist reported in September that a $650 million deal to redevelop Hunts Point — and eliminate the need for the trailers — had collapsed amid concerns from the co-op of produce operators at the market, which supplies as much as 60% of the city’s produce. The market, which sits on city-owned land, has for years relied on transport refrigeration units, also known as TRUs, to store produce because the facility’s 1960s-era warehouses are at capacity. The rumbling trailers are known for operating 24/7 at the site. Each trailer produces emissions equivalent to 330 truck trips on the Cross Bronx Expressway every day, according to the governor’s office. In his final days in office, previous Mayor Eric Adams announced the plan to modernize the Hunts Point market facility. But the deal fell apart this summer under Mayor Zohran Mamdani after market operators raised questions about whether the project might disrupt their operations. Sanchez’s bill applies to all stationary diesel-powered transport refrigeration units in large warehouses, food distribution centers, marine terminals and railyards across the city. Violators would face fines of up to $5,000. Hunts Point Produce Market relies on the refrigerated trailers for storage because warehouses are at capacity. “There is no reason why Hunts Point needs to suffer at the behest of being the food distribution hub of the city,” Sanchez said. The neighborhood, which is heavily trafficked by trucks, has some of the highest asthma rates in the country. Joel Fireman, a third-generation Hunts Point produce operator and co-president of the co-op, disputed the extent of the pollution and said the bill would only wind up hurting a major employer in the Bronx. He said the site currently has around 800 trailers, many of which run on both diesel and electric. But he said the market’s old infrastructure prevents operators from accessing more electricity. That is one of the major reasons city officials have encouraged the co-op to redevelop the facility.  “Environmentally we’re all in favor of cleaning up the market,” Fireman said. “Don’t put obstacles in our way. Come up with a solution.” The bill comes ahead of a Dec.16 City Council hearing, when members are expected to grill administration officials on why the Hunts Point deal collapsed. Mamdani has blamed his predecessor Eric Adams for rushing a deal before all parties agreed to the terms. He said the city is looking to “create a new path forward” but has not said whether the city can salvage the funding, which included $370 million in federal loans and grants. Officials, including city Comptroller Mark Levine, have urged City Hall to try to resurrect the project, saying, “We cannot let this fail.” Sanchez said his proposed legislation is intended to put pressure on everyone at the bargaining table. “We're not going to just let folks pollute our air indefinitely,” he said. The current lease between the city and Hunts Point co-op operators expires in 2039. If passed, the legislation would take effect two years after it becomes law. Sanchez said other U.S. municipalities have passed similar legislation. He said he is currently recruiting other council members to co-sponsor the bill. Cassio Mendoza, a spokesperson for Mamdani, said the mayor’s office would review the legislation. “The Mamdani administration remains committed to working with local stakeholders to identify solutions that reduce harmful emissions and improve the quality of life for Hunts Point residents,” he added in a statement. A spokesperson for Council Speaker Julie Menin’s office said she will review the bill once it is introduced. Tagged Elizabeth Kim is a reporter on the People and Power desk who covers mayoral power. She previously covered the pandemic, housing, redevelopment and public spaces. A native of Queens, she speaks fluent Mandarin. Got a tip? Author of the CMO Insider: Creator Brief newsletter Private equity is diving deeper into the creator economy. Falfurrias Capital Partners has made a majority investment in Freeman & Forrest, a firm that's helped Amazon, Google, and other tech companies use creators to reach technical customers, Business Insider exclusively learned. The deal price wasn't disclosed. Freeman & Forrest plans to use the capital to serve more Big Tech companies, as well as AI and cloud startups. It also plans to jump into other B2B categories such as the medical and defense sectors. Cofounder Emily Freeman will continue as CEO, while cofounder Forrest Brazeal will remain as president; both will be on the board. Also joining the board are ad industry vet and Falfurrias advisor Alex Jutkowitz, as executive chair, and Linda Boff, former global CMO of GE. Freeman and Brazeal founded the firm in 2024 after running influencer programs at companies like Microsoft and Google Cloud and finding that influencer marketing firms were designed for consumer brands, not B2B ones. Today, they say they work with one-third of the tech companies in the Fortune 100 across a network of more than 1,600 technical influencers. Its estimated annual revenue is about $50 million, per a person familiar with the company. Freeman said that while the 30-person firm has been doubling revenue every year, the capital infusion will help it expand faster by enabling it to hire more specialized account managers and developers to bolster its campaign-building platform. Private equity firms are playing a small but expanding role in funding creator economy companies as the sector matures, reflecting a growing recognition of the creator economy's potential. PE is directly or indirectly behind about 5% of all creator economy deals historically and about 8% of deals so far in 2026, according to estimates by Quartermast, an advisory firm. This month, H.I.G. Capital invested in Jake Rosen Entertainment, a talent firm, with plans for more deals. Earlier, Eldridge Industries invested in Fixated, a digital talent and content studio. US creator ad spend has grown four times as fast as media overall and is set to hit $44 billion this year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau estimated. What started as a medium focused on consumer brands is now accelerating in B2B. Forrester predicted that 75% of enterprise B2B companies would increase their influencer budgets in 2026 as trusted subject-matter experts play a bigger role in buying decisions. Freeman said B2B influencer marketing has nuances that set it apart from B2C. Personality is a big part of selling consumer products, and marketers often see an immediate impact on purchase decisions. B2B creator marketing puts more emphasis on expertise, and the sales cycle can be long. "Because the end user has a suspicion of anything that feels like a sales or marketing gimmick, you have to approach it as educational, making sure that the end user feels value from that content," Freeman said. The risk tolerance is also different. B2B brands tend to focus on making sure the creator follows FTC disclosure guidelines, doesn't use AI in a way that misrepresents the brand, and has the right persona. "We love influencers who are jalapeño-spicy, because it's interesting, but we don't want ghost-pepper-hot," Freeman said. "The definition of personality is a little different here." Chris Erwin, founder of RockWater, an M&A advisor for the creator economy, said the AI boom has fueled B2B creator marketing, as firms increasingly use creator economy channels to reach decision-makers. Erwin said he's had a growing number of conversations with firms representing tech and knowledge creators who speak to enterprise buyers, small to medium-sized businesses, and more. Erwin said investors are drawn to B2B because agencies have specialized skills, marketers' budgets are large and often renewed, and credible technical creators are scarce. "The trade-off is a smaller market, and specialist agencies are often built around founders who are the brand," he said. "Buyers will pay for the expertise, but want to see the business scale beyond the founders." Freeman said B2B is just getting started in adopting creator marketing, but that she sees the opportunity to expand to any field or company, whether it's an AI startup that's trying to grow awareness, an enterprise that's rebranding, or a company trying to get its expensive technology into the hands of end-users. "We're seeing demand grow at the same time that you're seeing these influencers start to really recognize that their industry expertise is what makes them a great influencer," she said. Jump to

As someone in their 20s, becoming a homeowner has always felt a bit out of reach for me. For the past few years, I've wanted to own something, live a simpler life, and make a smart financial decision. There was just one problem: beyond feeling like I couldn't afford to buy a traditional house or condo, I didn't want to have a mortgage or be responsible for a big space. I also didn't want to live in an apartment, since I'd be paying rent on something I didn't even own. So, to make this dream a reality, I started thinking about building my own place in my home state of Washington. I'd seen a lot of people my age online making the jump to live in a tiny home, and I decided this was going to be my next move. After looking at prices online, I thought it might be cheaper to build one from scratch than to buy a preassembled one. I proposed the idea to my dad, knowing I would need his help with physical labor to make this goal possible. He said yes, and from there I made the biggest purchase — the trailer bed that the home would sit on. With the money in my savings and labor assistance from some family members, I built the 224-square-foot home — with an extra 149 square feet of loft space. I also took on multiple jobs to help pay for the materials as the project continued. After nearly two years of building and roughly $45,000 spent, my home was complete. Unfortunately, this price tag was just the beginning, and now, nearly five years into living in my tiny home, I still haven't fully escaped the ongoing costs of homeownership. My tiny home is about the size of a standard studio apartment, but my friends have said it feels a lot bigger. Despite it being small, I've been able to make the most out of the space. I have a full-size kitchen, a bathroom with a washer and dryer, a full-size bed in my loft, an L-shaped couch, a large projector screen, and a garden outside. But even with a comfortable setup, owning a tiny home hasn't meant escaping housing costs.
