The biggest ongoing expense of living in the home is renting the land it sits on. Buying just a small piece of land seemed like a steep price, and since I wasn't able to get a personal loan, I decided to rent out a piece of property instead. Fortunately, I scored a great deal on a plot of land in the Seattle area that includes utilities, WiFi, garbage service, and lawn care — for $650 a month. Even though it's significantly cheaper than other options I found online, my rent alone has totaled roughly $39,000 over the past five years, on top of the $45,000 I spent to build the place. In addition to the property costs, I underestimated how expensive maintenance would be, even in such a small space. So far, I've resealed the wood siding, fixed a small leak in the roof, and swapped out the heated hose that supplies water to my house twice. I also have to change the water filters every three months. None of these expenses have been overwhelming on their own, but they add up over time. And unlike traditional renters, who can typically rely on a landlord to handle major repairs, I'm the only one responsible for keeping my home in good shape. It can be a lot for one person. For me, though, I'd rather handle the maintenance myself to save some money. When I take all this into account, I would still choose the tiny-house life, no matter the added expenses. Combining the build and the rent, I've spent roughly $84,000 in nearly five years — before accounting for maintenance and smaller repairs. For comparison, the average one-bedroom apartment in Washington state rents for roughly $1,800 a month. Over five years, that would add up to $108,000, which is significantly more than I've spent so far. For me, the appeal goes way deeper than the potential savings, though. I love being able to fully customize my space and own a place that is completely mine. I have a big vegetable garden, space for animals when the time is right, privacy, and a cozy design — all just in a few hundred square feet.  And I'm not giving up any comfort or conveniences, as people may expect — since the only major item I don't have is a dishwasher. I don't think I'll live in this house forever, but for the time being, I'm pretty happy with it. Depending on the market, I could eventually sell my home or, as I plan to, rent it out as a short-term rental for additional income. But for now, my low monthly property rent gives me financial freedom, so I can travel more, work less, and keep my expenses to a minimum. Tiny-house living came with expenses I didn't anticipate, but it has still been a worthwhile financial and lifestyle choice for me. Jump to

Senior Correspondent covering technology and culture Far be it from me to discourage anyone shopping for toys on Black Friday. I am staunchly pro-toy. Solidarity with kids! But please, I beg you — do not buy your kids an AI companion toy. There are plenty of reasons why not to, but the latest: NBC recently reported that several retailers removed listings for an AI talking toy after it was discovered to uh, have some problems: Target, Walmart, Macy's and Amazon have removed their listings for the toy. Two other plush toys with AI chatbots that the reporters tested had other problems — one would switch between English and Mandarin, and another that was advertised as good for kids with autism and helping preschoolers learn to spell would misspell words like "apple." To be fair, the toy that discussed gang rape and executions only did so when asked about the historical and current events like the Rohingya genocide or the 1940 Katyn massacre. It's less likely that young kids are asking about those things than nosy reporters who are specifically testing the toy's limits. This isn't the first time that AI toys have been discovered to have weird and troubling problems. Last year, consumer safety group PIRG put out a report saying that several AI toys on the market aimed at young kids would engage in sexual talk. Some of those same NBC reporters tested out some of those toys and found that they'd also give Chinese government talking points, like saying "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China." I've tested out an AI toy with my kids, a plush doll shaped like a cute rocket called "Grok" from the company Curio. I had ordered this because the singer Grimes, former romantic partner of Elon Musk, was part of the company early on and supplied the voice for Grok, which I found intriguing. (Confusingly, the toy has no relation to Musk's AI chatbot, Grok.) The toy, which launched in December 2023, was pretty early in the recent history of LLMs, and as you might imagine, it was a little clunky. There was a big latency problem — it would take a few seconds to respond to you, which led to constant crosstalk. It also seemed to not really do that much — you could ask it factual questions, or ask it to tell you a story, but this got old pretty quickly. My kids, who were 3 and 7 at the time, got bored of it in a day or two. Grok is currently living inside one of those bean bag chairs for less-loved stuffed animal storage.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  On the flip side, imagine your kids actually do love their AI toy. There's another possible downside: what happens if that toy gets discontinued and the support for the tech that powers it goes dark? That happened to people who bought the $800 Moxie robot, an early AI robot toy marketed as a social companion for kids. The company ran out of money and had to shut down, cutting off support for the product. I talked to a few owners of these toys at the time, who were bereft — some of their kids had really come to adore the toy and were upset that it stopped working. But really, the big question is if it's even a good idea for kids to be talking to a fuzzy cute AI plush toy at all. Sure, it's possible that an AI toy could help a child pursue their interests or practice language, social skills or even academics. But kids aren't as good as adults at understanding that a chatbot isn't "real" — and there are plenty of adults out there who believe they're in a romantic relationship with a chatbot. Talking toys have been around for decades (yes, I was very jealous of my peers how had a Teddy Ruxpin), but an AI toy is very, very different. There are few things more magical than walking into a dive bar at 2 pm on a Tuesday. It's late enough in the day to provide some plausible deniability but early enough to avoid the happy hour crowd. In the air hangs the stench of stale beer and decades-old cigarettes and the ghosts of drunken decisions past. Jimmy's Corner, tucked under an unassuming blue awning steps from Times Square, is the type of place built for those kinds of afternoons. Its walls are lined with photos and memorabilia gathered by its late owner, Jimmy Glenn, a longtime boxing trainer. The bar is heavily shellacked, its edges intermittently covered in duct tape. Above the liquor shelf hangs a sign warning that political talk is prohibited. In the corner sits a Knicks-branded foam finger covered in dust bunnies, a reminder of how long fans waited for the NBA championship. Beer cases are stacked at the back of the narrow space on the walk to the bathroom, which is appropriately covered in graffiti, though not terrifyingly gross. The November afternoon I walk into the 55-year-old establishment, it feels like traveling back in time, minus the paper straws. The man next to me at the bar agrees to watch my water while I scoot away for a minute, and I agree to only lightly make fun of him for drinking his Heineken over ice. Someone stops in to leave a phone battery for a guy named Phil. Regulars buy drinks for a trio of young sailors in town for the week before shooing them away to bars where they're likelier to meet women. Looming over all of it is the fact that the existence of Jimmy's Corner is at risk — it's locked in an eviction battle with a landlord that wants it out. For years, New Yorkers have fretted over the death of the dive — these neighborhood homes away from home that still feel homey. They remain resilient, but rising rents, soaring costs, and shifting drinking habits have left them in an extra precarious position. "New York needs but is in danger of losing authenticity and what really makes New York," says Jimmy's son, Adam Glenn, who now owns the bar. "I love this city, and part of it is why is anyone going to come if we just have the same stuff that every other place has?" Glenn always planned to return to Jimmy's Corner, despite his Harvard law education. He abandoned his corporate legal career to help run the bar in 2015, when his mother died of lung cancer, and fully took over when his father died of COVID complications in 2020 at the age of 89. In 2023, the building's owner — the Durst Organization — attempted to terminate the bar's lease, arguing that Jimmy Glenn's death voided it. Adam Glenn has sued to stop the eviction, alleging the clause allowing Durst to end the tenancy upon his father's death was slipped into a 2010 modification without his father's knowledge. He also points out that the landlord accepted his rent payments, which come out to about $5,000 a month, for years after his dad died — including during the 18 months the bar was closed due to the pandemic. Glenn isn't naive — he recognizes that keeping Jimmy's in its original location forever is not a realistic expectation. Durst sold the building this year, and the new owner appears to also want Jimmy's gone. For now, the best-case scenario is the bar makes it to the current lease's 2029 expiration date. "I didn't ever tell them, 'I'll never leave, I refuse to go,'" Glenn says. "There's a right way to do it, but you're choosing to do this in the ugliest way possible." A spokesperson for the Durst Organization said in an email that the building was sold and that they are no longer the landlord. An attorney for the new owner, Ben-Josef Group Holdings, did not respond to a request for comment. One of modern New York's paradoxes is that in a city of 8 million people, storefronts can sit empty for months or years while longtime businesses struggle to stay put. Bars and nightclubs have a 10.9% vacancy rate, according to the city comptroller, and in some Manhattan neighborhoods, vacancies can be especially persistent. Once a gritty block becomes desirable, a bar built on cheap drinks and loyal customers can find itself unable to make the new market-rate rent. It then becomes dependent on a landlord's willingness to renew a lease rather than attract a tenant with deeper pockets. "You're really at the mercy of the landlord," says Andrew Berman, the executive director of Village Preservation, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on Lower Manhattan. There are legal mechanisms for preserving buildings, he adds, but not for preserving a business. Of course, longtime establishments close for a multitude of reasons — their owners retire or sell, a new buyer decides to change the concept. But the losses become harder to write off as ordinary churn when a bar is still viable as a business, and the people running it are eager to keep going. A look at the 50 locations on Complex Magazine's 2011 list of New York City's best dive bars illustrates the evolving landscape. At least 10 have now closed, while others have moved, been renovated beyond recognition, or face their own lease and ownership threats. Plenty remain — dive bars are, indeed, stubborn institutions — but their endurance often depends on circumstances far beyond whether people still want to drink there. It's possible to come out on the other side of tumult. Take Neir's Tavern in Woodhaven, Queens. Loycent Gordon, a now-retired FDNY firefighter, bought Neir's in 2009 when it was on the brink of shuttering. The nearly 200-year-old neighborhood fixture had become a bit too divey for its changing surroundings — peeling paint, a crumbling tin ceiling, one draft beer on tap. "When I came in, I found that $200 for them on a Saturday night was a big deal," Gordon says. He made some adjustments, bringing in food and making the place more welcoming to a broader clientele, while maintaining the neighborhood vibe. The pivot worked until it didn't — a new landlord bought the building in 2018, and when the lease came up for renewal, they tried to jack up the rent. By early 2020, Neir's was once again on the brink of closing. As a Hail Mary, Gordon called into Mayor Bill de Blasio's weekly radio show to ask for help, and after some municipal cajoling, the parties were able to reach a deal that both the landlord and tenant could stomach. Still, staying afloat has become a war of attrition. "It's like death from a thousand cuts," Gordon says. Rent may be the most visible threat, but bars are being squeezed simultaneously from all sides. Wholesale prices for everything from liquor to frying oil are up, while labor costs are marching steadily higher. Few customers pay with cash anymore, meaning credit card swipe fees shave off the top of every tab. The real "sleeper," Gordon says, is liability insurance. His provider tried to cancel his relatively affordable policy a couple of months ago, and he had to "fight like hell" to keep it. If a big hike had happened, he would have had to fire some of his employees. Gordon sees Neir's as a "beacon of hope and stability in an ever-changing world," but it's not stagnant, as Gordon sets out to diversify revenue streams. He has signed contracts with tourist companies to try to bring visitors in — one of the bar's claims to fame is that it was featured prominently in "Goodfellas." He is working on a plan to distribute one of its signature drinks at retail locations, and he's licensed two Neir's outposts at JFK Airport. The challenges keep on coming. The nightlife industry depends heavily on foreign workers, and the Trump administration's crackdown has spooked many immigrants. One of Gordon's longtime employees is Mexican, and while he's living and working fully legally in the US, he refused to go to the new JFK location to help with training out of fear he could be mistakenly detained by federal immigration authorities. "He was scared to death," Gordon says. The adversity dive bars are facing isn't confined to New York. John Bodnovich, the executive director of American Beverage Licensees, a trade association for alcohol retailers, says that while many locals across the country are hanging in there, the business remains a grind. Margins are razor-thin, and customers are increasingly selective about where they spend their money. Many Americans are drinking less, choosing to moderate for the sake of their health and their bank accounts. GLP-1s are curbing alcohol consumption, and THC drinks are eating into some market share. Gen Z is still figuring out bar culture. This environment requires owners to get creative and "give people a reason to show up," Bodnovich says. That might mean bingo, trivia, or karaoke, or hammering home for customers what makes the place unique. "Of local neighborhood bars that are successful, they have a personality, and they have a character — they develop that," he says. Even for local bars that have personality and character in spades, so much comes down to who controls the real estate. In the life of a city, there's always a balance to strike between nostalgia and progress, including back at Jimmy's Corner. "I grew up here in the 'bad old days' of Times Square," Glenn says. It's good that some of the city's roughest edges have been sanded down. That's also what makes his situation so frustrating. "Part of what made it better was my parents being out here and protecting people and making sure that this little corner of Times Square was safer than it was before they got here," he says. But improving a neighborhood drives up property values and makes other, larger businesses more willing to come in. Jimmy's still manages to sell $3 beer, which Glenn prefers to think of not as cheap but accessible. "That's how New York's supposed to be," he says. "You're supposed to have rich, poor, black, white, local, tourists, all in the same place." Glenn has started scoping out other locations for a move, but he's found he doesn't have much leverage with landlords who seem content to let their properties sit empty. His real dream is to buy a space of his own, so that he, not a landlord, can control his own destiny. For all the uncertainty, Glenn's enjoyed running Jimmy's more this year than he has since his parents passed. You always appreciate things more when you might lose them, and even the little annoyances take on a certain charm. He plans to host a party at Jimmy's on December 4 to mark the one-year anniversary of his lawsuit, which is still making its way through the court. "It's like getting another day with a family member or someone you love," Glenn says. "I get to be here." Emily Stewart is a senior correspondent at Business Insider, writing about business and the economy. Jack Newsham contributed reporting for this story. Most Americans have returned to the office at least some days a week, and with them come the glory days of the long commute. Business Insider analyzed the Census Bureau's 2025 American Community Survey data to find the 20 US metropolitan areas with the longest travel times to work. The Census defines a metro as consisting of counties associated with an urban area of at least 50,000 people, plus adjacent counties with strong social and economic ties to the core. The data showed that the mean one-way commute time in the US was 27.4 minutes in 2025, with metros in Maryland, New York, and California among the worst. That's higher than in recent years, with the average commute at 27.2 minutes in 2024 and 26.8 minutes in 2023.  The data applies to workers aged 16 and older who did not work from home and includes workers who drove alone or carpooled, used public transportation, walked, biked, or used another mode of transportation.  Much of this shift comes amid sweeping RTO mandates. Major companies across the country have called thousands of employees back to the office for up to five days a week in recent years. About 87% of workers reported commuting to a workplace in the Census data. People also now live farther from work, moving away when the pandemic hit in search of cheaper housing, and many haven't moved back. In 2019, the mean distance employees traveled to their offices was 15 miles, according to data from the National Bureau of Economic Research. By 2024, that rose to 26 miles.  Here are the top metros where Americans spent the most time commuting. Workers in the Miami metro area spent an average of 30.6 minutes commuting to work. About 9.7% of workers reported carpooling, compared with 69.1% who drove alone. Workers in the Hagerstown metro area also had an average commute of 30.6 minutes. About 10.2% of workers worked from home, while nearly 76.4% drove alone. Workers in Hammond spent an average of 30.7 minutes getting to work. Chicago-area workers spent an average of 30.9 minutes commuting to work. Public transportation was the usual way of getting to work for 9.3% of workers. The average commute in the Los Angeles metro area was 31 minutes. Driving was overwhelmingly the preferred mode of transportation: 69% of workers drove alone, and 9% carpooled. Commuters in the Modesto metro area, in California's Central Valley, spent an average of 31.3 minutes on their way to work. Fewer than 1% of workers used public transportation, while 78.8% drove to work alone. The average commute in the Houston metro area was 31.3 minutes. Driving was the most popular mode of transportation: 72.2% of workers drove alone, and another 10.7% carpooled. Baltimore's average commute in 2025 came out to 31.6 minutes. About 70.6% of workers drove alone, 7.2% carpooled, and 3.8% of workers used public transportation. Workers in the Cape Coral metro area also had an average commute of 31.8 minutes. Driving alone accounted for 71.4% of workers' usual commutes, while just 0.4% took public transportation. The average commute in the greater Boston area was 31.9 minutes. Boston had one of the list’s more varied transportation mixes: 10.5% of workers used public transportation and 4.8% walked to work. Workers in the Atlanta metro area spent an average of 32.4 minutes commuting. About 68.8% still reported driving alone. The average commute in the San Francisco metro area was 32.5 minutes. It had the largest share of bicycle commuters on the list, at 1.6%, and 11.6% of workers took public transportation. The average commute in the Lakeland metro area was 32.5 minutes. About 68.6% of workers drove alone to work, while 11.9% carpooled. The average commute in the Bridgeport metro area was 33.3 minutes. About 63.7% of workers drove alone, while 9.2% used public transportation. Workers in the Kiryas Joel–Poughkeepsie–Newburgh metro area spent an average of 33.7 minutes commuting. Walking was the usual way of getting to work for 3.9% of workers, compared with 9.2% who used public transportation. The average commute in the Washington metro area was 34.3 minutes. It also had one of the highest work-from-home rates among the metros ranked, at 17.4%. The average commute in California's Inland Empire was 34.6 minutes. About 12% of workers carpooled — among the highest shares in the ranking — while 74.2% drove alone. Workers in Stockton–Lodi also spent an average of 35.6 minutes commuting. More than 14% carpooled, while 1.8% used public transportation. The New York metro area had the country’s second-longest average commute, at 36.8 minutes. It stood apart from the rest of the ranking in its reliance on public transportation: 28.2% of workers commuted by transit, while 44.6% drove alone. Workers in Lexington Park spent an average of 39.4 minutes commuting, the longest commute among the metros the Census reported by nearly three minutes. About 78.4% of workers drove alone, and only 0.8% used public transportation. Jump to

CEO Dario Amodei and six co-founders, who together own about 10 per cent of the frontier AI firm, have stakes now valued at around $US225 billion combined. Investors are watching whether the AI company's enormous valuation can be sustained amid growing concerns about the AI sector. Shares in Anthropic have surged in their Wall Street debut, briefly pushing the artificial intelligence company's market value above $US2 trillion ($3 trillion), overtaking SpaceX's debut. The maker of the Claude AI chatbot opened at $US111.50 ($167) on the Nasdaq, a 34 per cent jump from its initial public offering price of $US83, as investors rushed to buy into the first major frontier AI company to list on a stock exchange. The debut marked a major milestone for the AI industry, but the initial excitement faded as investors took profits and its shares gave up some of the early gains. The main US indexes also retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. The stock, trading under the ticker ANT, was last quoted at $US96.30, as at 7am AEDT. Claude is a series of large language models developed by Anthropic and used worldwide. (Supplied: Anthropic) Anthropic raised $US81.3 billion through its IPO, alongside a further $US26 billion in a concurrent private placement involving major technology companies. The listing comes at a turbulent time for the technology sector, which has been rattled by concerns of an AI bubble, worries over mounting debt among data centre operators and a widening scandal that forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to step down as CEO. Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap, said she had expected Anthropic's debut to help revive enthusiasm for AI stocks, but that had failed to materialise. "I think tomorrow you will probably see the stock dropping in the red, there certainly seems like there's enough demand, but the price is still too high." Australian investors were among a select group outside the United States given the opportunity to buy shares in Anthropic before its stock market debut. Commonwealth Bank-owned CommSec was appointed the lead Australian retail broker, with investors also able to apply through participating brokers including Stake and Sharesies. CommBank also stands to benefit from Anthropic's success, having invested in the AI company in 2025. According to its latest annual report, the value of CBA's stake had climbed to $1.53 billion by the end of June, up from $153 million a year earlier. CommSec and Sharesies declined to comment when asked about demand among Australian retail investors. Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said his firm's grey market indicators had pointed to a strong debut for Anthropic. The indicator allows traders to speculate on a company's share price before it officially hits the stock exchange, providing an early indication of investor expectations. The investment boom behind AI is looking increasingly shaky just as it is about to revolutionise our lives.  "If you sort of use that as a rough guide, demand's been really strong," he said. Mr Rodda compared the excitement to the launch of a new iPhone. "People lining up around the streets to be some of the first people to get their hands on it," he said. "It's very, very much a similar sort of psychology dynamic amongst investors." Ms Liu from Ten Cap said strong demand for Anthropic shares was partly due to their limited availability, with relatively few shares being offered to investors. Ms Liu believes Anthropic is a "great company" but has decided against buying shares at the current valuation. "It's just too expensive," she said. "It's yet to make money so you're paying a lot for a company based on what they can achieve, they still need to get there. "Remember, they still have to achieve it." She said the company's shares would start to look very attractive to her if its share price fell about 20–30 per cent from listing price. xAI's Colossus 1 data centre in Memphis, Tennessee — now in partnership with Anthropic — houses more than 220,000 NVIDIA GPUs. (Supplied: Steve Jone/Flight by Southwings for SELC) Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, Anthropic has experienced explosive growth, with revenue surging 13-fold to $US33.2 billion in the first nine months of this year, driven largely by businesses adopting its AI products, particularly Claude Code. But despite this, Anthropic is still losing money, reporting an operating loss of $US1.26 billion over the same period, highlighting the enormous costs of developing and running advanced AI models. The company also faces significant costs as it expands, with around $US900 billion in long-term spending commitments, largely tied to computing power and infrastructure needed to develop as well as run its AI models. Investors are also buying into a company where the seven co-founders will retain a majority (50.1 per cent) of shareholder voting power, limiting the influence of shareholders over major decisions. Daniel Newman, chief executive of US technology research firm Futurum Group, said the broader AI industry still faced some difficult questions despite Anthropic's record float. He pointed to high interest rates, persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty weighing on technology stocks, even as demand for AI continues to grow. "Nvidia's strong earnings didn't save the AI trade. Anthropic's IPO probably won't save it either," he said. Fortunes are made by entrepreneurs and investors when revolutionary technologies enable waves of innovative, investable companies. Think of the railroad, the Bessemer process, electric power, the internal combustion engine, or the microprocessor—each of which, like a stray spark in a fireworks factory, set off decades of follow-on innovations, permeated every part of society, and catapulted a new set of inventors and investors into power, influence, and wealth. Yet some technological innovations, though societally transformative, generate little in the way of new wealth; instead, they reinforce the status quo. Fifteen years before the microprocessor, another revolutionary idea, shipping containerization, arrived at a less propitious time, when technological advancement was a Red Queen’s race, and inventors and investors were left no better off for non-stop running. Anyone who invests in the new new thing must answer two questions: First, how much value will this innovation create? And second, who will capture it? Information and communication technology (ICT) was a revolution whose value was captured by startups and led to thousands of newly rich founders, employees, and investors. In contrast, shipping containerization was a revolution whose value was spread so thin that in the end, it made only a single founder temporarily rich and only a single investor a little bit richer. Is generative AI more like the former or the latter? Will it be the basis of many future industrial fortunes, or a net loser for the investment community as a whole, with a few zero-sum winners here and there? There are ways to make money investing in the fruits of AI, but they will depend on assuming the latter—that it is once again a less propitious time for inventors and investors, that AI model builders and application companies will eventually compete each other into an oligopoly, and that the gains from AI will accrue not to its builders but to customers. A lot of the money pouring into AI is therefore being invested in the wrong places, and aside from a couple of lucky early investors, those who make money will be the ones with the foresight to get out early. The microprocessor was revolutionary, but the people who invented it at Intel in 1971 did not see it that way—they just wanted to avoid designing desktop calculator chipsets from scratch every time. But outsiders realized they could use the microprocessor to build their own personal computers, and enthusiasts did. Thousands of tinkerers found configurations and uses that Intel never dreamed of. This distributed and permissionless invention kicked off a “great surge of development,” as the economist Carlota Perez calls it, triggered by technology but driven by economic and societal forces.[1] There was no real demand for personal computers in the early 1970s; they were expensive toys. But the experimenters laid the technical groundwork and built a community. Then, around 1975, a step-change in the cost of microprocessors made the personal computer market viable. The Intel 8080 had an initial list price of $360 ($2,300 in today’s dollars). MITS could barely turn a profit on its Altair at a bulk price of $75 each ($490 today). But when MOS Technologies started selling its 6502 for $25 ($150 today), Steve Wozniak could afford to build a prototype Apple. The 6502 and the similarly priced Zilog Z80 forced Intel’s prices down. The nascent PC community started spawning entrepreneurs and a score of companies appeared, each with a slightly different product. You couldn’t have known in the mid-1970s that the PC (and PC-like products, such as ATMs, POS terminals, smartphones, etc.) would revolutionize everything. While Steve Jobs was telling investors that every household would someday have a personal computer (a wild underestimate, as it turned out), others questioned the need for personal computers at all. As late as 1979, Apple’s ads didn’t tell you what a personal computer could do—it asked what you did with it.[2] The established computer manufacturers (IBM, HP, DEC) had no interest in a product their customers weren’t asking for. Nobody “needed” a computer, and so PCs weren’t bought—they were sold. Flashy startups like Apple and Sinclair used hype to get noticed, while companies with footholds in consumer electronics like Atari, Commodore, and Tandy/RadioShack used strong retail connections to put their PCs in front of potential customers.  The market grew slowly at first, accelerating only as experiments led to practical applications like the spreadsheet, introduced in 1979. As use grew, observation of use caused a reduction in uncertainty, leading to more adoption in a self-reinforcing cycle. This kind of gathering momentum takes time in every technological wave: It took almost 30 years for electricity to reach half of American households, for example, and it took about the same amount of time for personal computers.[3] When a technological revolution changes everything, it takes a huge amount of innovation, investment, storytelling, time, and plain old work. It also sucks up all the money and talent available. Like Kuhn’s paradigms in science, any technology not part of the wave’s techno-economic paradigm will seem like a sideshow.[4] Source: [3] The nascent growth of PCs attracted investors—venture capitalists—who started making risky bets on new companies. This development incentivized more inventors, entrepreneurs, and researchers, which in turn drew in more speculative capital. Companies like IBM, the computing behemoth before the PC, saw poor relative performance. They didn’t believe the PC could survive long enough to become capable in their market and didn’t care about new, small markets that wanted a cheaper solution. Retroactively, we give the PC pioneers the powers of prophets rather than visionaries. But at the time, nobody outside of a small group of early adopters paid any attention. Establishment media like The New York Times didn’t take the PC seriously until after IBM’s was introduced in August 1981. In the entire year of 1976, when Apple Computer was founded, the NYT mentioned PCs only four times.[5] Apparently, only the crazy ones, the misfits, the rebels, and the troublemakers were paying attention. Source: [5] It’s the element of surprise that should strike us most forcefully when we compare the early days of the computer revolution to today. No one took note of personal computers in the 1970s. In 2025, AI is all we seem to talk about. Big companies hate surprises. That’s why uncertainty makes a perfect moat for startups. Apple would never have survived IBM entering the market in 1979, and only lived to compete another day after raising $100 million in its 1980 IPO. It was the only remaining competitor after the IBM-induced winnowing.[6] Source: [6] As the tech took hold and started to show promise, innovations in software, memory, and peripherals like floppy disk drives and modems joined it. They reinforced one another, with each advance putting pressure on the technologies adjacent to it. When any part of the system held back the other parts, investors rushed to fund that sector. As increases in PC memory allowed more complicated software, for example, there became a need for more external storage, which caused VC Dave Marquardt to invest in disk drive manufacturer Seagate in 1980. Seagate gave Marquardt a 40x return when it went public in 1981. Other investors noticed, and some $270 million was plowed into the industry in the following three years.[7] Money also poured into the underlying infrastructure—fiber optic networks, chip making, etc.—so that capacity was never a bottleneck. Companies which used the new technological system to outperform incumbents began to take market share, and even staid competitors realized they needed to adopt the new thing or die. The hype became a froth which became an investment bubble: the dot-com frenzy of the late 1990s. The ICT wave was therefore similar to previous ones—like the investment mania of the 1830s and the Roaring ‘20s, which followed the infrastructure buildout of canals and railways, respectively—in which the human response to each stage predictably generated the next. When the dot-com bubble popped, society found it disapproved of the excesses in the sector and governments found they had the popular support to reassert authority over the tech companies and their investors. This put a brake on the madness. Instead of the reckless innovation of the bubble, companies started to expand into proven markets, and financiers moved from speculating to investing. Entrepreneurs began to focus on finding applications rather than on innovating the underlying technologies. Technological improvements continued, but change became more evolutionary than revolutionary. As change slowed, companies gained the confidence to invest for the longer term. They began to combine various parts of the system in new ways to create value for a wider group of users. The massive overbuilding of fiber optic telecom networks and other infrastructure during the frenzy left plenty of cheap capacity, keeping the costs of expansion down. It was a great time to be a businessperson and investor. In contrast, society did not need a bubble to pop to start excoriating AI. Given that the backlash to tech has been going on for a decade, this seems normal to us. But the AI backlash differs from the general high regard, earlier in the cycle, enjoyed by the likes of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, and others who built big tech businesses. The world hates change, and only gave tech a pass in the ‘80s and ‘90s because it all still seemed reversible: it could be made to go away if it turned out badly. This gave the early computer innovators some leeway to experiment. Now that everyone knows computers are here to stay, AI is not allowed the same wait-and-see attitude. It is seen as part of the ICT revolution. Perez, the economist, breaks each technological wave into four predictable phases: irruption, frenzy, synergy, and maturity. Each has a characteristic investment profile. The middle two, frenzy and synergy, are the easy ones for investors. Frenzy is when everyone piles in and investors are rewarded for taking big risks on unproven ideas, culminating in the bubble, when paper profits disappear. When rationality returns, the synergy phase begins, as companies make their products usable and productive for a wide array of users. Synergy pays those who are patient, picky, and can bring more than just money to the table. Irruption and maturity are more difficult to invest in. Investing in the 1970s was harder than it might look in hindsight. To invest from 1971 through 1975, you had to be either a true believer or a conglomerator with a knuckle-headed diversification strategy. Intel was a great investment, though it looked at first like a previous-wave electronics company. MOS Technologies was founded in 1969 to compete with Texas Instruments but sold a majority of itself to Allen-Bradley to stay afloat. Zilog was funded in 1975 by Exxon (Exxon!). Apple was a great investment, but it had none of the hallmarks of what VCs look for, as the PC was still a solution in search of a problem. It was later irruption, in the early 1980s, when great opportunities proliferated: PC makers (Compaq, Dell), software and operating systems (Microsoft, Electronic Arts, Adobe), peripherals (Seagate), workstations (Sun), and computer stores (Businessland), among others. If you invested in the winners, you did well. But there was still more money than ideas, which meant that it was no golden age for investing. By 1983, there were more than 70 companies competing in the disk drive sector alone, and valuations collapsed. There were plenty of people whose fortunes were established in the 1970s and 1980s, and many VCs made their names in that era. But the biggest advantage to being an irruption-stage investor was building institutional knowledge to invest early and well in the frenzy and synergy phases. Investing in the maturity phase is even more difficult. In irruption, it’s hard to see what will happen; in maturity, nothing much happens at all. The uncertainty about what will work and how customers and society will react is almost gone. Things are predictable, and everyone acts predictably. The lack of dynamism allows the successful synergy companies to remain entrenched (see: the Nifty 50 and FAANG), but growth becomes harder. They start to enter each other’s markets, conglomerate, raise prices, and cut costs. The era of products priced to entice new customers ends, and quality suffers. The big companies continue to embrace the idea of revolutionary innovation, but feel the need to control how their advances are used. R&D spending is redirected from product and process innovation toward increasingly fruitless attempts to find ways to extend the current paradigm. Companies frame this as a drive to win, but it’s really a fear of losing. Innovation can happen during maturity, sometimes spectacularly. But because these innovations only find support if they fit into the current wave’s paradigm, they are easily captured in the dominant companies’ gravity wells. This means making money as an entrepreneur or investor in them is almost impossible. Generative AI is clearly being captured by the dominant ICT companies, which raises the question of whether this time will be different for inventors and investors—a different question from whether AI itself is a revolutionary technology. Shipping containerization was a late-wave innovation that changed the world, kicked off our modern era of globalization, resulted in profound changes to society and the economy, and contributed to rapid growth in well-being. But there were, perhaps, only one or two people who made real money investing in it. The year 1956 was late in the previous wave. But that year, the company soon to be known as SeaLand revolutionized freight shipping with the launch of the first containership, the Ideal-X. SeaLand’s founder, Malcom McLean, had an epiphany that the job to be done by truckers, railroads, and shipping lines was to move goods from shipper to destination, not to drive trucks, fill boxcars, or lade boats. SeaLand allowed freight to transfer seamlessly from one mode to another, saving time, making shipping more predictable, and cutting costs—both the costs of loading, unloading, and reloading, and the cost of a ship sitting idly in port as it was loaded and unloaded.[8] The benefits of containerization, if it could be made to happen, were obvious. Everybody could see the efficiencies, and customers don’t care how something gets to where they can buy it, as long as it does. But longshoremen would lose work, politicians would lose the votes of those who lost work, port authorities would lose the support of the politicians, federal regulators would be blamed for adverse consequences, railroads might lose freight to shipping lines, shipping lines might lose freight to new shipping lines, and it would all cost a mint. Most thought McLean would never be able to make it work. McLean squeezed through the cracks of the opposition he faced. He bought and retrofitted war surplus ships, lowering costs. He went after the coastal shipping trade, a dying business in the age of the new interstates, to avoid competition. He set up shop in Newark, NJ, rather than the shipping hub of Hell’s Kitchen, to get buy-in from the port authority and avoid Manhattan congestion. And he made a deal with the New York longshoremen’s union, which was only possible because he was a small player whom they figured was not a threat. Source: [10] But competitors and regulators moved too quickly for McLean to seize the few barriers to entry that might have been available to him: domination of the ports, exclusive agreements with shippers or other forms of transportation, standardization on proprietary technology, etc.[9] When it started to look like it might work, around 1965, the obvious advantages of containerization meant that every large shipping line entered the business, and competition took off. Even though containerized freight was less than 1% of total trade by 1968, the number of containerships was already ramping fast.[10] Capacity outstripped demand for years.  The increase in competition led to a rate war, which led to squeezed profits, which in turn led to consolidation and cartels. Meanwhile, the cost of building ever-larger container ships and the port facilities to deal with them meant the business became hugely capital intensive. McLean saw the writing on the wall and sold SeaLand to R.J. Reynolds in January 1969. He was, perhaps, the only entrepreneur to get out unscathed. It took a long time for the end-to-end vision to be realized. But around 1980, a dramatic drop began in the cost of sea freight.[11] This contributed to a boom in international trade,[12] and allowed manufacturers to move away from higher-wage to lower-wage countries, making containerization irreversible. Source: [11] Some people did make money, of course; someone always does. McLean did, as did shipping magnate Daniel Ludwig, who had invested $8.5 million in SeaLand’s predecessor, McLean Industries, at $8.50 per share in 1965 and sold in 1969 for $50 per share.[13] Shipbuilders made money, too: between 1967 and 1972, some $10 billion ($80 billion in 2025 dollars) was spent building containerships. The contractors that built the new container ports also made money. And, later, shipping lines that consolidated and dominated the business, like Maersk and Evergreen, became very large. But, “for R.J. Reynolds, and for other companies that had chased fast growth by buying into container shipping in the late 1960s, their investments brought little but disappointment.”[14] Aside from McLean and Ludwig, it is hard to find anyone who became rich from containerization itself, because competition and capex costs made it hard to grow fast or achieve high margins. Source: [12] The business ended up being dominated primarily by the previous incumbents, and the margins went to the companies shipping goods, not the ones they shipped through. Companies like IKEA benefited from cheap shipping, going from a provincial Scandinavian company in 1972 to the world’s largest furniture retailer by 2008; container shipping was a perfect fit for IKEA’s flat-pack furniture. Others, like Walmart, used the predictability enabled by containerization to lower inventory and its associated costs. With hindsight, it’s easy to see how you could have invested in containerization: not in the container shipping industry itself, but in the industries that benefited from containerization. But even here, the success of companies like Walmart, Costco, and Target was coupled with the failure of others. The fallout from containerization set Sears and Woolworth on downward spirals, put the final nail in the coffin of Montgomery Ward and A&P, and drove Macy’s into bankruptcy before it was rescued and downsized by Federated. Meanwhile, in North Carolina, “the furniture capital of the world,” furniture makers tried to compete with IKEA by importing cheap pieces from China. They ended up being replaced by their suppliers.[15] If there had been more time to build moats, there might have been a few dominant containerization companies, and the people behind them would be at the top of the Forbes 400, while their investors would be legendary. But moats take time to build and, unlike the personal computer, the adoption of containerization wasn’t a surprise—every business with interests at stake had a strategic plan immediately. The economist Joseph Schumpeter said “perfect competition is and always has been temporarily suspended whenever anything new is being introduced.”[16] But containerization shows this isn’t true at the end of tech waves. And because there is no economic profit during perfect competition, there is no money to be made by innovators during maturity. Like containerization, the introduction of AI did not lead to a period of protected profits for its innovators. It led to an immediate competitive free-for-all. Let’s grant that generative AI is revolutionary (but also that, as is becoming increasingly clear, this particular tech is now already in an evolutionary stage). It will create a lot of value for the economy, and investors hope to capture some of it. When, who, and how depends on whether AI is the end of the ICT wave, or the beginning of a new one.  If AI had started a new wave, there would have been an extended period of uncertainty and experimentation. There would have been a population of early adopters experimenting with their own models. When thousands or millions of tinkerers use the tech to solve problems in entirely new ways, its uses proliferate. But because they are using models owned by the big AI companies, their ability to fully experiment is limited to what’s allowed by the incumbents, who have no desire to permit an extended challenge to the status quo. This doesn’t mean AI can’t start the next technological revolution. It might, if experimentation becomes cheap, distributed and permissionless—like Wozniak cobbling together computers in his garage, Ford building his first internal combustion engine in his kitchen, or Trevithick building his high-pressure steam engine as soon as James Watt’s patents expired. When any would-be innovator can build and train an LLM on their laptop and put it to use in any way their imagination dictates, it might be the seed of the next big set of changes—something revolutionary rather than evolutionary. But until and unless that happens, there can be no irruption. AI is instead the epitome of the ICT wave. The computing visionaries of the 1960s set out to build a machine that could think, which their successors eventually did, by extending gains in algorithms, chips, data, and data center infrastructure. Like containerization, AI is an extension of something that came before, and therefore no one is surprised by what it can and will do. In the 1970s, it took time for people to wrap their heads around the desirability of powerful and ubiquitous computing. But in 2025, machines that think better than previous machines are easy for people to understand. Consider the extent to which the progress of AI rhymes with the business evolution of containerization: In the “AI rhymes” column, the first four items are already underway. How you should invest depends on whether you believe Nos. 5–7 are next. Economists are predicting that AI will increase global GDP somewhere between 1%[17] to more than 7%[18] over the next decade, which is $1–7 trillion of new value created. The big question is where that money will stick as it flows through the value chain. Most AI market overviews have a score or more categories, breaking each of them into customer and industry served. But these will change dramatically over the next few years. You could, instead, just follow the money to simplify the taxonomy of companies: What the history of containerization suggests is that, if you aren’t already an investor in a model company, you shouldn’t bother. Sam Altman and a few other early movers may make a fortune, as McLean and Ludwig did. But the huge costs of building and running a model, coupled with intense competition, means there will, in the end, be only a few companies, each funded and owned by the largest tech companies. If you’re already an investor, congratulations: There will be consolidation, so you might get an exit. Domain-specific models—like Cursor or Harvey—will be part of the consolidation. These are probably the most valuable models. But fine-tuning is relatively cheap, and there are big economies of scope. On the other hand, just as Google had to buy Invite Media in 2010 to figure out how to sell to ad agencies, domain-specific model companies that have earned the trust of their customers will be prime acquisition targets. And although it seems possible that models which generate things other than language—like Midjourney or Runway—might use their somewhat different architecture to carve out a separate technological path, the LLM companies have easily entered this space as well. Whether this applies to companies like Osmo remains to be seen. While it’s too late to invest in the model companies, the profusion of those using the models to solve specific problems is ongoing: Perplexity, InflectionAI, Writer, Abridge, and a hundred others. But if any of these become very valuable, the model companies will take their earnings, either through discriminatory pricing or vertical integration. Success, in other words, will mean defeat—always a bad thesis. At some point, model companies and app companies will converge: There will simply be AI companies, and only a few of them. There will be some winners, as always, but investments in the app layer as a whole will lose money.  The same caveat applies, however: If an app company can build a customer base or an amazing team, it might be acquired. But these companies aren’t really technology companies at all; they are building a market on spec and have to be priced as such. A further caveat is that there will be investors who make a killing arbitraging FOMO-panicked acquirors willing to massively overpay. But this is not really “investing.” There might be an investment opportunity in companies that manage the interface between the AI giants and their customers, or protect company data from the model companies—like Hugging Face or Glean—because these businesses are by nature independent of the models. But no analogue in the post-containerization shipping market became very large. Even the successful intermediation companies in the AI space will likely end up mid-sized because the model companies will not allow them to gain strategic leverage—another consequence of the absence of surprise. When an industry is going to be big but there is uncertainty about how it will play out, it often makes sense to swim upstream to the industry’s suppliers. In the case of AI, this means the chip providers, data companies, and cloud/data center companies: SambaNova, Scale AI, and Lambda, as well as those that have been around for a long time, like Nvidia and Bloomberg. The case for data is mixed. General data—i.e., things most people know, including everything anyone knew more than, say, 10 years ago, and most of what was learned after that—is a commodity. There may be room for a few companies to do the grunt work of collating and tagging it, but since the collating and tagging might best be done by AI itself, there will not be a lot of pricing leverage. Domain-specific models will need specialist data, and other models will try to answer questions about the current moment. Specific, timely, and hard to reproduce data will be valuable. This is not a new market, of course—Bloomberg and others have done well by it. A more concentrated customer base will lower prices for this data, while wider use will raise revenues. On balance, this will probably be a plus for the industry, though not a huge one. There will be new companies built, but only a couple worth investing in. The high capex of AI companies will primarily be spent with the infrastructure companies. These companies are already valued with this expectation, so there won’t be an upside surprise. But consider that shipbuilding benefited from containerization from 1965 until demand collapsed after about 1973.[19] If AI companies consolidate or otherwise act in concert, even a slight downturn that forces them to conserve cash could turn into a serious, sudden, and long-lasting decline in infrastructure spending. This would leave companies like Nvidia and its emerging competitors—who must all make long-term commitments to suppliers and for capacity expansion—unable to lower costs to match the new, smaller market size. Companies priced for an s-curve are overpriced if there’s a peak and decline. Source: [19] All of which means that investors shouldn’t swim upstream, but fish downstream: companies whose products rely on achieving high-quality results from somewhat ambiguous information will see increased productivity and higher profits. These sectors include professional services, healthcare, education, financial services, and creative services, which together account for between a third and a half of global GDP and have not seen much increased productivity from automation. AI can help lower costs, but as with containerization, how individual businesses incorporate lower costs into their strategies—and what they decide to do with the savings—will determine success. To put it bluntly, using cost savings to increase profits rather than grow revenue is a loser’s game. The companies that will benefit most rapidly are those whose strategies are already conditional on lowering costs. IKEA’s longtime strategy was to sell quality furniture for low prices and make it up on volume. After containerization made it possible for them to go worldwide, IKEA became the world’s largest retailer and Ingvar Kamprad (the IK of IKEA) became a billionaire. Similarly, Walmart, whose strategy was high volume and low prices in underserved markets, benefited from both cost savings and just-in-time supply chains, allowing increased product variety and lower inventory costs. Today’s knowledge-work companies that already prioritize the same values are the least risky way to bet on AI, but new companies will form or re-form with a high-volume, low-cost strategy, just as Costco did in the early 1980s. New companies will compete with the incumbents, but with a clean slate and hindsight. Regardless, there are few barriers to entry, so each of these firms will face stiff competition and operate in fragmented markets. Experienced management and flawless execution will be key. Being an entrepreneur will be a fabulous proposition in these sectors. Being an investor will be harder. Companies will not need much private capital—IKEA never needed to raise risk capital, and Costco raised only one round in 1983 before going public in 1985—because implementing cost-savings technology is not capital intensive. As with containerization, there will be a long lag between technology trigger and the best investments. The opportunities will be later. Stock pickers will also make money, but they need to be choosy. At the high end of projections, an additional 7% in GDP growth over 10 years within one third of the economy gives a tailwind of only about 2% per year to these companies—even less if productivity growth from older ICT products abates. The primary value shift will be to companies that are embracing the strategic implications of AI from companies that are not, the way Walmart benefited from Sears, which took advantage of cheaper goods prices but did not reinvent itself. Consumers, however, will be the biggest beneficiaries. Previous waves of mechanization benefited labor productivity in manufacturing, driving prices down and saving consumers money. But increased labor productivity in manufacturing also led to higher manufacturing wages. Wages in services businesses had to rise to compete, even though these businesses did not benefit from productivity gains. This caused the price of services to rise.[20] The share of household spending on food and clothing went from 55% in 1918 to 16% in 2023,[21] but the cost of knowledge-intensive services like healthcare and education have grown well above inflation.  Something similar will happen with AI: Knowledge-intensive services will get cheaper, allowing consumers to buy more of them, while services that require person-to-person interaction will get more expensive, taking up a greater percentage of household spending. This points to obvious opportunities in both. But the big news is that most of the new value created by AI will be captured by consumers, who should see a wider variety of knowledge-intensive goods at reasonable prices, and wider and more affordable access to services like medical care, education, and advice. There is nothing better than the beginning of a new wave, when the opportunities to envision, invent, and build world-changing companies leads to money, fame, and glory. But there is nothing more dangerous for investors and entrepreneurs than wishful thinking. The lessons learned from investing in tech over the last 50 years are not the right ones to apply now. The way to invest in AI is to think through the implications of knowledge workers becoming more efficient, to imagine what markets this efficiency unlocks, and to invest in those. For decades, the way to make money was to bet on what the new thing was. Now, you have to bet on the opportunities it opens up. The US blockade of Iranian ports is having a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive. Save Share Tehran, Iran – Iran’s economy is expected to contract further due to the ongoing blockade of its ports by the United States, inflicting pain on tens of millions of Iranians. But experts say it is too early to tell whether Washington’s economic embargo on Tehran is having the desired outcome of either collapsing the Iranian government or forcing it to concede to US demands. The US believes its naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and sanctions – part of its maximum pressure campaign on Tehran – are working. The US has also brought a third aircraft carrier into the region to support a potential military escalation, in what appears to be an attempt to force Tehran to capitulate further to its demands. After a deadlock in the US-Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on February 28, Washington has demanded Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and curb its nuclear programme. However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure and have put forward their demands. Strikes on US interests in the region this week, including radar systems in Bahrain, have been viewed as a defiant response to the US military and economic pressure. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions. Tehran-based economist Peyman Molavi said if current conditions persist, Iran’s inflation could rise considerably over the coming months. “This will impact parallel markets like foreign currencies, gold, the stock market and housing,” he told Al Jazeera. “But it will unfortunately have the largest impact on the commodities market, from energy to agricultural products, metals, and industrial products.” For decades, Iran’s governments have increasingly plugged their budget deficits by printing more money, which has saddled the country with a growing money supply, feeding chronic inflation. The foreign currency crunch from disrupted oil exports due to the US military blockade has only exacerbated the situation. Molavi estimates that the year-on-year growth of the money supply in Iran could rise to 55-60 percent from its current figure of nearly 51 percent by the end of the Persian year in late March. Paired with negative economic growth, he said annual inflation could grow to about 85 percent, and point-to-point inflation to 100 percent. Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati hit back at US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran. “Like I said, he must still count his chickens at the end of autumn before moving to winter,” he said in reference to an Iranian proverb – “It’s too early to talk about winter”. Bessent has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027. Iran’s official figures indicated that the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar year. Hemmati said the central bank has secured $30bn in foreign currencies to weather the pressure over the coming months, prioritising procurement of essential goods for its citizens. “American officials believe they can achieve their goals through threats and raise something new each time; from the possibility of collapse to military threats and intensified economic pressure,” Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said on Sunday. All overland routes to and from Iran, except for one with Iraq that was closed due to security reasons, remain open despite the US efforts to isolate Iran from its neighbours, Madanizadeh insisted. For the seventh Iranian month of Mehr that ended on October 22, the 12-month average annual inflation was at 76.8 percent, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran. Point-to-point inflation, which compares just that month with the same month of the previous year, was at 88.7 percent. Essential goods have already been experiencing triple-digit inflation for months, with the category of food, beverages and tobacco experiencing year-on-year inflation of 113.4 percent in October, the centre said. Iranian social media is increasingly filled with personal stories of how most people in the country of about 90 million are rapidly losing their purchasing power. “Everywhere you look, you could have bought the same commodity with one-fifth of the money last year,” one user wrote on X. “That’s no joke, millions of people have been crushed in between.”      Saleh, a 37-year-old shopkeeper at Tehran’s Grand Bazaar who deals in electric motors for small industrial units, said both domestic and Chinese-made goods can still readily be found in the market. But supply and demand have decreased since US sanctions began to bite. “The reason is that commodities are expensive, and there’s been a stagnation in the market and also uncertainty over what will happen next,” he told Al Jazeera, asking not to use his full name due to security reasons. “Everyone’s looking at the dollar price, and manufacturers and clients are making their decisions based on price changes. If we sold 10 items before, now we’re selling three or four, but the price increase maintained some profit. I don’t see the market being near collapse, but there’s less business.” Companies with an established client base are proving more resilient, he added. Bessent hailed what is happening in Iran as “one of the fastest collapses in history”, and described the Trump-directed sanctions campaign against Iran as “the greatest economic isolation in the history of the world against a single country”. He also compared the situation in Iran with the period preceding the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, saying the country’s economy had shrunk 22 percent over three years before the union collapsed. Economist Molavi said the comparison may not necessarily translate into immediate economic collapse for Iran as they have fundamentally different economic models. But he pointed out that Iran’s nominal GDP has fallen from $645bn in 2012 to about $300bn now and that it could decline further if the sanctions continue. “With the current [level] of underinvestment, halted oil sales, disrupted exports and the sense of suspension in the economy, our economic growth will become even more negative,” he said. Author of the First Trade newsletter Anthropic's IPO is officially a record-breaker. The Claude maker priced its offering at $83 a share, raising about $107 billion and landing at a fully diluted valuation of $1.5 trillion. That total includes a separate $26 billion private placement at the offer price, making it the biggest US IPO ever by deal size. While those rankings capture the unprecedented scale of the offering, they don't tell us what's next. And what's next could redefine the AI trade as we know it. When Anthropic starts trading under the "ANT" ticker later today, it'll be the public market's first opportunity to constantly monitor a company that's become a stand-in for the AI industry's biggest hopes. In the weeks leading up to the debut, investors have gotten a better handle on how much money Anthropic makes — and how much it is committed to spend to keep building. Now, the stock's first days of trading could help answer three other key questions that the IPO price alone cannot: This is not a typical IPO built around share scarcity. Anthropic is bringing an enormous amount of stock to the market, even before accounting for the $26 billion private placement with Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC. That makes today's debut less about whether Anthropic can generate a splashy opening print than whether it can find a durable trading level. A huge first-day pop could signal intense demand — and so could a more orderly debut that holds its ground after an opening frenzy. Either outcome would matter more than a fleeting headline number. Anthropic's AI-trade consortium of investors has already supplied a powerful vote of confidence. These are the companies that sell the chips, cloud capacity, and infrastructure needed to power AI. Now they're also helping to finance one of their biggest customers. Farmers are receiving higher payments but are producing far less milk and also face rising prices for hay. Save Share Nairobi, Kenya – Milk is becoming harder to find in parts of Kenya as prolonged dry conditions take a toll on dairy farmers, disrupting supplies to major towns and pushing up prices. In Nairobi, some popular brands have become increasingly difficult to find in shops. A 500ml (1-pint) packet of Tuzo, Dairy Best or Mt Kenya milk sells for 79 to 89 Kenyan shillings ($0.61 to $0.68), but supplies have been limited. New brands have appeared on supermarket shelves at about 65 shillings ($0.50) while some neighbourhood shops visited by Al Jazeera were charging as much as 100 shillings ($0.77) for the same quantity.     The shortage is being felt across the dairy supply chain, from farmers struggling to feed their animals to businesses that depend on a steady supply of fresh milk. In Kajiado County, southwest of Nairobi, dairy farmers said a prolonged dry spell has sharply reduced milk production over the past three months. Jennifer Leshinka, a farmer in Bisil, told Al Jazeera that her daily milk production had fallen from 120 litres (32 gallons) to 50 litres (13 gallons). With natural pasture dwindling, she has had to buy hay to feed her animals. Some of her dairy animals have also been moved to neighbouring counties in search of grazing land. “I supplement the little natural grass with several bales of hay to feed my animals, which has become expensive. A bale of hay is currently retailing between 100 and 150 shillings [$0.77 to $1.15], yet it cannot sustain a mature animal for a day,” Leshinka said. The pressure is not limited to Kajiado. Diminishing pasture and water supplies are affecting pastoralists in arid and semiarid areas as well as dairy farmers in the highlands, another important milk-producing region. Jackson Sinkeet, a farmer who supplies raw milk to hotels across the Nairobi metropolitan area, said falling yields have made it difficult to meet orders, even from customers willing to pay higher prices. He warned that the situation could worsen if dry conditions persist. The decline in production is also affecting dairy cooperatives, which collect milk from farmers and supply major processors. Jeremiah Ole Ncharo, Kajiado County’s executive committee member in charge of cooperatives, told Al Jazeera that at least five major women-led dairy cooperatives have reported a 50 percent drop in milk deliveries from their members during the dry period. He said the reduced volumes were affecting supplies to large milk processors, adding to pressure on the formal market. In Nairobi, hotelier Joram Kamau said businesses were spending hours queuing at major processors’ depots to obtain rationed milk. The shortage has also raised concerns about the products available in the market. Kamau said he was worried about the growing presence of powdered milk products whose quality and authenticity he questioned. He said he would rather wait for genuine milk, even if it cost more, than risk buying questionable products and losing customers. Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the current shortage was largely linked to prolonged dry conditions, which have reduced the availability of pasture, fodder and water, affecting animal productivity and the amount of milk delivered to processors. He said Kenya’s dairy industry has continued to grow with national milk production rising from 4.64 billion kilogrammes (10.23 billion pounds) in 2021 to 5.52 billion kilogrammes (12.17 billion pounds) in 2025. Formal milk deliveries also increased from about 802 million litres (212 million gallons) to 1.01 billion litres (267 million gallons) over the same period. However, more recent figures point to a decline in milk reaching formal processors. Kagwe said monthly deliveries averaged about 83.45 million litres (22 million gallons) in 2025, compared with 74.09 million litres (19.57 million gallons) in September. He said the decline has affected volumes available for processing, particularly UHT milk, which has a longer shelf life and helps maintain supplies. However, government market surveillance for the week ending October 30 indicated a slight improvement in UHT milk availability across most parts of the country. Other dairy products, including fermented milk, butter and cheese, were generally available at normal stock levels. Kagwe said the government was monitoring production, processor stocks, producer prices and retail prices. It was also facilitating regional transfers of milk and dairy products, particularly within the East African Community, while encouraging processors to collect more milk from farmers and cooperatives. He added that farmers were receiving better prices amid tighter supplies. The average gross producer price rose to about 53.88 shillings ($0.41) per litre (1 quart) in July, compared with an average of 49.58 shillings ($0.38) in 2025. To address longer-term challenges in the dairy sector, the government is looking at ways to increase production and improve farmers’ resilience. Kagwe said planned measures included expanding fodder production and conservation, continuing a subsidised artificial insemination programme to improve dairy genetics and distributing milk coolers to organised farmer groups. The restructuring of the state-owned dairy processor New KCC is also expected to improve services to producers and consumers. The government is also exploring President William Ruto’s proposal to introduce Indian water buffaloes to Kenya as an additional source of milk. Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the initiative was still at an early stage. Kenya would first need to establish veterinary and import requirements, identify suitable breeds and sources, and bring in a limited number of animals to assess their adaptability and productivity under local conditions. India, the world’s largest milk producer, relies on buffaloes for about 43 percent of its milk production. Buffalo milk has a relatively high fat and solids content, making it suitable for products such as cheese and butter. But Kagwe said the proposal should be seen as a medium- to long-term opportunity rather than a response to the current shortage. For farmers such as Leshinka and Sinkeet, the immediate challenge remains the rising cost of keeping their animals fed and productive. In Nairobi, businesses are still struggling to secure enough milk to meet customer demand. “The animals’ milk yield has dropped significantly. I am unable to supply my customers, who are willing to pay higher prices, because the milk is simply not available,” Sinkeet told Al Jazeera.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition. That’s because the movement of ad budgets from linear to streaming has hardly been evenly paced. Streaming’s share of ad revenue is indeed growing at major media companies, including The Walt Disney Company, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. But their earnings tell a different story: Linear revenue is falling faster than streaming revenue is rising. The shift is happening, but it’s not benefiting content owners as expected. The core problem is a supply-demand imbalance. Streaming ad revenue is growing through increased volume, not higher prices. New inventory floods in, making cheap inventory abundant. As major subscription services continue to promote free ad-supported streaming tiers, the buyers’ market will only continue. The solution is to grow demand, not increase prices. Fortunately, the ad dollars needed to support the streaming market already exist, sitting in local and midmarket budgets that haven’t been able to buy national CTV efficiently. The opportunity is to bring these advertisers into the broader video and streaming market, then develop ways to keep them investing. Correcting the imbalance requires creating new demand, then ensuring that content quality and product performance are strong enough to eventually shift pricing dynamics. When it comes to growth, the glut of cheap national SVOD supply may be a problem for programmers, but it’s an opportunity for local and midmarket advertisers. If the current streaming market is largely aimed at Fortune 500 companies, the industry has to consider the thousands of smaller advertisers that make steady annual investments in local linear buys. Taken collectively, these advertisers represent billions of dollars in ad budgets. Because these advertisers have smaller budgets, many haven’t tried streaming. It is more cost-efficient for them to execute local and spot buys on linear than to invest in targeted or national streaming campaigns. These advertisers are still seeing real success reaching millions of linear viewers, so they understand the power of TV. They just need an entry point for CTV. Solving this issue would allow demand to flow steadily into the market. Once that demand enters the market, additional steps must happen. CPMs fall when inventory is sold as undifferentiated tonnage. With platforms like Disney+ and Netflix exploring free ad-supported tiers, even more low-cost supply will enter the market. But cheap supply that doesn’t perform isn’t worth an advertiser’s investment. If that inventory doesn’t deliver results for advertisers outside the Fortune 500, those advertisers will invest their budgets elsewhere, creating another demand imbalance. The answer lies in household addressability. While this is available on some streaming platforms, it’s still largely absent from the overall TV market, including linear. Household-level addressability turns cheap impressions into targeted impressions worth buying, even within highly premium inventory. The more information brands have about who will see their ads and whether those ads are likely to resonate with the viewer, the more they are likely to pay. It is no secret that streaming is the future of TV, and shifting revenue numbers reflect that. To build a sustainable future for media companies and advertisers, the entire ecosystem must first provide ease of access and then addressability. Making streaming easier to buy at scale would help solve the demand problem. Once more advertisers are in the market, addressability creates greater competition for impressions, solving the pricing imbalance. This future is out there, provided the industry takes a few steps in the right direction.
