When I first became interested in cooking, I spent a lot of time watching Ina Garten on Food Network and diving into her cookbooks and recipes. To me, Garten is one of the greats — so when I decided to cook an early Thanksgiving dinner for friends, it was a no-brainer that I'd put together a menu full of "Barefoot Contessa" recipes. Like Garten, I kept things simple and elegant, choosing classics like roasted turkey, mashed potatoes, and green beans. Although I've been cooking Thanksgiving dinner for my family for over 15 years, I learned new tricks and found recipes I would definitely make again. Here's what it was like to cook a full-on Garten-giving. Still, since I was following recipes from a pro, I thought I'd probably have to go to four or five different grocery stores or specialty shops to gather all of the ingredients. However, my grocery list was actually simple, with lots of easy-for-me-to-acquire items like fresh green beans, tomatoes, elbow macaroni, tomatoes, butter, and goat cheese. To my surprise, I found everything I needed at Walmart on a single trip. Garten's deep-dish apple pie was to be our dessert, so I made it a day in advance to save time later. The recipe called for a lot of citrus zest, but it was simple to get the amount I needed from oranges and lemons using my microplane grater. It also required me to peel, quarter, and core several pounds of Granny Smith apples, which was time-consuming but not difficult. I'm pretty die-hard about following recipes, but I cheated a little on this one by using a store-bought pie crust rather than making my own. I was glad I did, as making the pie was still a lot of work. I prepped Garten's make-ahead cranberry sauce the day before, too. I've made cranberry sauce from scratch before, but I prefer the canned variety, so I was curious how Garten's would stack up. The recipe called for tart Granny Smith apples, fresh cranberries, and lots of citrus zest, which required a lot of grating and chopping. My microplane was already getting a lot of use — this was now the second zest-filled recipe from Garten I followed. Day one of cooking also involved making Garten's goat-cheese mashed potatoes. Since the mashed-potato recipe was full of creamy butter and milk, adding goat cheese seemed odd to me, but who am I to argue with the Barefoot Contessa? I prepped the entire recipe ahead of the big day — whipping my potatoes with a hand mixer, loading the cheesy mixture into a baking pan, and then topping it with butter and Parmesan. Tomorrow, I'd just need to heat the potatoes up. Garten's sausage-and-herb stuffing was next on my to-do list. I also prepped this a day in advance. The recipe was simple and super straightforward. I cubed my bread, toasted it, then tossed it in the buttery celery, apple, onion, and parsley mixture. In a separate pan, I browned my sausage, then added it to my bread cubes along with cranberries and chicken stock. The dish came together easily and was ready to be baked the next day. My kids would riot if mac and cheese wasn't part of our Thanksgiving meal, so I chose a Garten recipe with a tomato topping to mix up our usual side. In addition to topping the Gruyère-and-cheddar-based mac with fresh tomatoes, the recipe also called for a fresh breadcrumb topping. I'd never made fresh breadcrumbs before, but I quickly learned just how easy it is. I just put slices of bread into a food processor and pulsed.  In no time, this mac and cheese was already ready for the fridge. One of my favorite ways to keep things organized while cooking a big meal like this is to cover each pre-assembled dish with aluminum foil and write the cooking time and temperature on top with a permanent marker. That way, when it's time to cook, I can easily see what needs to go into the oven and for how long. I won't have to search for the recipes again to find the information. Garten's green-beans gremolata recipe is a big jump from my normal casserole, but I was excited to try a fresher, less creamy approach to the vegetable side.  Like a lot of Garten's Thanksgiving recipes, the gremolata calls for lots of citrus zest. I also needed ingredients like pine nuts, fresh herbs, and Parmesan. After blanching the green beans and placing them in an ice bath, I set them aside until they were ready to be sautéed and tossed with the gremolata just before serving. In recent years, my husband and I have spatchcocked our turkey, a technique in which you open the bird, remove the backbone, and lay it flat for cooking. It can help the turkey cook more quickly. We were hesitant to try Garten's oven-roasted turkey, as it was a way more traditional approach. After prepping the bird and stuffing it with garlic, herbs, onion, and lemon, we popped it into the oven and hoped for the best. I spent about 10 hours in the kitchen in total prepping our Thanksgiving menu, and when I saw everything put together, I knew the time was well worth it. Although Garten's Thanksgiving dinner didn't look like my usual one, it was stunning when everything came out of the oven and was laid out on my kitchen island. All of the dishes looked delicious and elegant. I immediately thought this was one of the most beautiful meals I'd made in my life. Garten's oven-roast turkey was beautiful and looked like something out of a Thanksgiving movie. Still, I think I'd stick with the spatchcocking method, which lets me plan my meal better. With the bird laid flat, I think it's easier to predict how long it'll take to reach the correct internal temperature. I'm still a canned cranberry sauce girl through and through. Garten's recipe was the most involved cranberry sauce I've ever made from scratch, with its citrus zest and chopped apples. It took a lot of work to make, and I don't feel the effort was worth it.  It tasted a bit too tart, and in the future, I'd happily stick with the canned stuff. I loved Garten's mashed potatoes, but adding an ingredient as creamy and tangy as goat cheese really changed their flavor profile. This was not your classic crowd-pleaser side dish. Rather, these mashed potatoes had pungent, tangy notes from the goat cheese that I could see some people not loving. Although the potatoes didn't scream "Thanksgiving" to me, I'd make them again as a side dish for a different meal. They had good flavor, and I did really like how creamy they were. I've never been into stuffing, as it's always seemed to lack flavor and take up valuable real estate in my stomach that I'd rather fill with the aforementioned green-bean casserole. Garten's stuffing recipe, however, made me a convert. I loved the freshly-made toasted cubes of bread we'd prepped the day before. And the savory sausage and herbs mixed with the tartness of the apples created a perfect flavor combo. I wasn't really sure about topping mac and cheese with fresh tomatoes, but it turned out to be a great idea. When combined with cheese and tomato, the homemade breadcrumbs and elbow macaroni provided enough carbs to give everyone at my dinner table grilled-cheese-and-tomato-soup vibes. I'm a big fan of traditional green-bean casserole made with cream-of-mushroom soup and crispy onions. Garten's green-beans gremolata was a different dish entirely — fresh and citrusy instead of creamy and full of umami. It was delicious, but different. I'd definitely make the side again, just not for Thanksgiving. Everyone thoroughly enjoyed Garten's deep-dish apple pie, so much so that it was the only menu item we didn't have leftovers of. Between the crispy crust and tart apples, the pie was the perfect balance of sweet and tangy. We served each slice with a scoop of vanilla-bean ice cream — the perfect accompaniment. Going on a 10-hour adventure through some of Garten's most iconic recipes was a lot of fun. Looking back, I'm still proud of my hard work and the beautiful menu I served my guests as a result. At the time, I spent $132.77 on ingredients, which felt like a solid deal considering I was able to feed a dozen people — and had leftovers. My usual Thanksgiving meals typically cost me a bit more to prepare. It was a lot of work,  but I found some great recipes I plan to make again throughout the year or for our next holiday feast.  This story was originally published on November 9, 2023, and most recently updated on November 18, 2026. Watch CBS News  Updated on:  November 19, 2026 / 5:39 PM EST             / CBS News            Public anxiety over a string of technology failures is driving some Americans to plan for the worst.  Jittery shoppers are stocking up on generators, shelf-stable canned goods, bottled water and other disaster-planning supplies at retailers such as Costco and Walmart, according to businesses and Wall Street analysts.  What's usually perceived as fringe behavior is starting to spread into the mainstream, according to RBC Capital Markets retail analyst Steven Shemesh.  "We've seen some evidence of it happening across the consumer retail space," he told CBS News, citing recent concurrent tech outages affecting online banking platforms, the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system and even the National Security Agency. "Right now, on the margins, people are preparing more than they have in the past." "People want to be comfortable knowing that if we did have an outage for a couple of days, they'd have food in the house," Shemesh added. Data from market research and analytics firm Circana show that purchases of common emergency-prep staples rose for the four weeks ending Nov. 1. Sales of water germicidal tablets, which remove contaminants from drinking water, surged 154% compared with the same period a year ago. Sales of disinfecting wipes rose 72%, while moist towelette sales increased 20%, according to data from RBC Capital Markets. Shemesh said that Walmart, which reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday, told RBC that it is seeing a spike in sales of doomsday staples such as soup, water and ready-to-eat foods. "It's not enough to move the needle for a company that does $8 billion in sales per year, but they are seeing those kinds of behaviors play out," Shemesh said. "Things could need to escalate quite a bit for this to go from level one to level three, which would maybe start to move the needle for some companies."  Nik Modi, global consumer and retail research co-head at RBC Capital Markets, is also seeing signs of panic shopping by consumers. "A convergence of government action and social media anxiety has pushed 'doomsday prepping' into mainstream consumer behavior over the past several months," Modi said in a research note this week.  He traces the shift in purchasing behavior to a Pentagon military readiness initiative in late September that was misinterpreted and amplified on social media as an impending "blackout."  Government officials have said the recent tech incidents are not connected and were not caused by cyberattacks. "The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday during a news conference in the Philippines.  Yet many consumers aren't taking any chances. Earlier this week, investment firm Mizuho Securities said that consumers flocked to Costco after tech vulnerabilities heightened concerns about the risk of a major cybersecurity incident.  "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report. He added that shoppers are "pantry-loading" and also depleting the retailer's inventory of "high-ticket generators," which were sold out online as of Sunday night.  Tractor Supply, which sells a range of tools, clothing, and heating and cooling equipment, told CBS News that it has seen increased demand across "several preparedness-related categories." It's selling more generators, liquid storage tanks, propane and accessory tanks than it did during the same period last year.         Edited by                                                                            Alain  Sherter  In:        © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc. Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting. President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand. Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse." The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied. Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.  Here are takeaways from Trump's trip: The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals. Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit. "As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable." "It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said. Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon. "It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said. In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security." Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. "We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said. For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks. "Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator. The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy. The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows. There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict. Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body. "In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks. As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction." OpenAI has reportedly picked the same company that assembles iPhones for its first phone. A report on Sohu, citing supply chain sources, says Foxconn subsidiary FIH Mobile has won an order to take part in assembling the finished phones. Foxconn is already Apple’s main iPhone assembler. Product plans, order size, and mass production arrangements are still unknown, the report says. If an OpenAI phone eventually goes on sale, the company would enter the smartphone market and could compete more directly with today’s phone brands around AI interaction. For now, ChatGPT still lives as an app on phones other companies make. OpenAI has officially discussed hardware with former Apple design chief John Ive after the IO team merged with the company in 2025, but it has not announced a smartphone. Once flawless, Apple now feels… off. What happened? On April 27, 2026, well-known analyst Ming-Chi Kuo said that OpenAI was working with MediaTek and Qualcomm on smartphone processors, with Luxshare as the exclusive system co-design and manufacturing partner. He expected mass production in 2028, and said specifications and suppliers would be finalized by late 2026 or the first quarter of 2027. Kuo argued that only by controlling both the operating system and the hardware could OpenAI deliver a full AI agent service, because a phone is the device that captures a user’s real-time state. He updated that view on May 5, 2026, saying OpenAI appeared to be fast-tracking the project, with mass production targeted as early as the first half of 2027. MediaTek, he wrote, looked better placed to become the sole processor supplier, using a customized Dimensity 9600 built on TSMC’s N2P process. He also listed a dual-NPU design, LPDDR6 memory, UFS 5.0 storage, and an image signal processor meant to improve real-world visual sensing. If development stayed on track, Kuo estimated combined 2027 and 2028 shipments could reach around 30 million units. The new Sohu report does not mention Luxshare, chips, or volumes, and it doesn’t call FIH Mobile the exclusive manufacturer, only a participant in assembly. In his April note, Kuo had already said Luxshare would struggle to overtake Hon Hai, Foxconn’s parent, in Apple’s assembly chain. If this report holds, that same group’s phone-making arm is now said to be lining up OpenAI’s assembly work. We want to hear from you. By   	Elisabeth Garber-Paul   	On Tuesday, more than two dozen veterans organizations sent an open letter to bipartisan congressional leaders demanding something that a few years ago might have been unheard of: better access to legal weed. “Veterans have sacrificed for our country, and they deserve safe, responsible options for managing chronic pain, PTSD, anxiety, sleep problems, and other health conditions,” it read. “Many veterans… rely on hemp products as an alternative to opioids. If Congress fails to act, the products they depend on will suddenly become illegal.”  	That’s because on Dec. 11, a new law that limits the amount of THC allowed in hemp will go into effect, eradicating the cannabis market as Americans have come to know it. The colorful cans of THC sodas on Trader Joe’s shelves will be gone, as will the sleep-aid gummies from Target and and the bottles of THC “liquor” at Total Wines. “Anyone who produces the seed, grows a crop, processes the crop, makes a product, sells it to the shelf, and the people who buy it — all these people will be impacted,” explains Greg Serrao, co-founder of Willie’s Remedy, one of the country’s best-selling cannabis drinks.  	           	The new definition will close an eight-year loophole that allowed the CBD market to take off, followed by the federally legal THC market. Veterans, farmers, and cannabis entrepreneurs agree that more regulations are needed to help finally wrangle what was, for a long time, a frontier industry. “A lot of people paint this picture of hemp as this wild west,” says Serrao. “That’s not true.”  	What is true is that unless Congress acts to amend the new rules, in less than a month, a $28 billion industry will disappear. “Something like 65 percent of our customers are senior citizens, and 70 percent are over 45,” says Willie’s Remedy’s other co-founder, Forrest Dein.   	Sens. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) introduced a bill to the Senate on Tuesday that would halt the new rules, instead offering a new set of regulations around hemp-derived THC products, including age limits, testing and packaging requirements, and other guardrails around the plant. “Our bill will put every bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating products out of the hands of children,” Sheehy, a veteran, said in a press release. “It will also stop Congress from turning the farmers, veterans, and cancer patients who rely on these products into criminals overnight.”  	            	 		Editor’s picks 	 	            	 	 		 					The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far		 	               	 	 		 					The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					100 Best Movies of the 21st Century		 	         	But unless that advances soon, the businesses who rely on hemp — including the struggling farmers who were told hemp would be the crop to save them — will be shit out of luck.  “The collateral damage is that we axe this American commodity that has so much hope,” explains Morgan Tweet, who runs IND Hemp, a company that processes hemp into products like rope and fiber. “It’s really something special for American farmers, and for American businesses, and manufacturers. There’s nothing in our generation that comes close to being able to show the potential that hemp has with how diverse and how useful of a crop it is, and the magnitude of products you can make from it.”  	It all started back in 2018, when Sen. Mitch McConnell accidentally legalized weed — kind of.  	On Dec. 20, 2018, President Donald Trump signed the Agricultural Improvement Act, colloquially known as the Farm Bill, into law. In between protections for dairy farmers and changes to the federal food assistance program was a monumental change: for the first time since 1937, growing hemp would be legal in the United States. McConnell himself championed the change, positioning it as a boon to farmers in his home state of Kentucky. The text of the bill defined hemp as a cannabis plant that contained no more than .3 percent delta-nine THC, weed’s intoxicating compound, on a dry-weight basis. “I do not have any plans to endorse the legalization of marijuana,” McConnell said, noting that hemp and marijuana were “two separate plants.”      	 		Related Content 	 	       	 	 		 					Summer Walker Files $20 Million Cross-Complaint Against Interscope		 	          	 	 		 					Julio Iglesias Under Investigation for Sexual Abuse Claims		 	          	 	 		 					What I Learned About Genocide From the Rohingya Muslims		 	          	 	 		 					Mullin Says Skipping LSU Game Amid FAA Crisis Would Have Caused ‘Confusion’		 	         	By then, hemp was already a popular crop in Europe, where it had long been used for everything from oil to rope. It was also at the center of the growing CBD industry. CBD, another cannabinoid found in hemp, was not intoxicating, like THC, but was starting to be used medicinally for things like epilepsy and pain management.  	Once hemp was legalized, American farmers started planting the crop. Some varieties focused on bushy leaves and heavy stalks, great for industrial uses. But others had big flowers, perfect for extracting CBD. The CBD boom was expected; what wasn’t was that scientists quickly figured out a process to convert CBD into THC — and the hemp-derived THC market took off. Not only did they figure out how to make delta-9 THC, the cannabinoid that is known to get us high, they also started to make a wide variety of other kinds of cannabinoids, including delta-8 THC (a slightly less potent intoxicant that is present in trace amounts in the plant), as well as some that don’t actually occur naturally. It was all legal because the products were derived from hemp, not marijuana, which is a Schedule I controlled substance.  	           	Many of these companies self-policed, testing the products themselves and going through established liquor frameworks in order to be sold at national chains. Others, however, skirted the rules, offering shady products made with questionable cannabinoids and no real testing or oversight. This so-called “gas station weed” started to make folks nervous — particularly McConnell. So when Congress was putting together a bill to reopen the government last fall, after a record-long shutdown, McConnell added an amendment to the 2018 definition of hemp to get rid of the market as we know it.  	The new law will change the definition of legal hemp. Previously, hemp was allowed to have up to .3 percent THC as measured in its dry weight. Hemp farmers could grow crops that adhered to this, then processors could extract cannabinoids, and companies put them into products so that they had enough potency to see effects. The new law, however, looks at the final product, restricting anything with more than .4 milligrams of THC per container.   	There are two parts to the law, explains Neil M. Willner, an attorney with Vicente LLP, a New York-based firm specializing in cannabis law. The first went into effect on Nov. 12, and banned the sale of all synthetic THC products, or THC compounds that are not found naturally in the cannabis plant. On Dec. 11, the low-dose sodas, liquors, and gummies that have become so popular — and usually contain five or 10 mg of THC per serving — will no longer be legal on a federal level. People in areas with state-legal cannabis programs can still go to a dispensary to buy THC products, but the companies built around hemp-derived cannabinoids — and the people in states without legal weed — will be out of luck.   	It will also make it nearly impossible to grow hemp, too. “We’ve talked to a lot of hemp farmers, and it’s very difficult for them to manage the THC content of their crops,” says Dein. “It’ll push a lot of farmers out of business.” Tweet, owner of IND Hemp, the processing facility, adds that the new law doesn’t define what a “container” actually is. “I ship 55-gallon drums of hemp seed oil all over the country, and by definition, that’s a container, right?” she says. “Like, we do make a product that likely will go above that 0.4 milligram [limit] just because of that volume. Even though hemp seed oil doesn’t have a lot of cannabinoids in it, it does have some, and so there is some risk to our business.”   	           	In one word, bad. Take, for example, Texas, where outgoing Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick introduced a bill over the summer that would have banned all hemp products that contained THC. This was wildly unpopular with many of the 1.5 million veterans who live in the state, among others. Outgoing Governor Greg Abbott ended up vetoing the bill, instead establishing guidelines for age and marketing restrictions. In November, Patrick lost his bid for reelection, as did Abbott and other Republicans statewide. “I think that’s one of the reasons Texas went blue,” says Serrao.  	Tim Jensen, CEO of the consulting firm War Party Inc., which advises companies on how best to connect with veterans, as well as a signatory to the open letter sent to Congress, points out that it’s more than bad optics — there’s a very real health risk to veterans if the rug is pulled out from under the industry. “We have a large community of individuals of 55 and older that are experiencing a lot of inflammation and pain-related problems that are wanting to find alternative modalities that are not opioid related, and that is big,” he says. “You’re finding the veteran community really leaning into these opportunities to get away from alcohol.”      	 		Trending Stories 	 	       	 	 		 					John Mayer Transports Michael J. Fox Back to the Future With Chuck Berry Performance		 	          	 	 		 					Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis		 	          	 	 		 					CMA Awards 2026: The Complete Winners List		 	          	 	 		 					Halestorm, Brothers Osborne, Hardy Sing for Brooks & Dunn at Ferocious 2026 CMA Tribute		 	         	Everyone who spoke to Rolling Stone for this article agreed that further federal regulations are needed in order for the industry to safely grow. Getting rid of full synthetics, as the law did on Nov. 12, is a positive step, they say, but “what we don’t have is purity standards,” explains Tweet. “We don’t have any regulations, so it’s only the people that self-regulate, that put good products on the market that are the ones you should be trusting. But the reality is that consumers have no idea what’s in their product. They don’t know what they’re buying.”  	Willie Nelson, himself a longtime cannabis outlaw, would like to see regulation come to the industry, rather than a step backward to prohibition. “I was born the year Prohibition ended, in 1933, and we know that approach does not work,” he tells Rolling Stone in a statement. “This ban punishes the wrong people. It hurts the family farmers growing a legal crop, and it hurts the millions of seniors, veterans, and patients who rely on hemp products for pain relief, sleep, and wellness. Congress needs to regulate this industry for safety, not destroy it.” We want to hear it. Send us a tip using our anonymous form. The AI company behind Claude raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering ever, at a $1.5 trillion valuation. Save Share Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, despite fears that AI could threaten humanity, protests over energy-hungry data centres and concerns about an AI investment bubble. Five years ago, Anthropic raised $124m from its first investors. On Wednesday, it priced its shares at $83 each, valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion and making it the world’s 12th-biggest company, just behind Tesla. Its shares begin trading on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.     Demand far outstripped expectations. Investors reportedly sought six times as many shares as were available, and Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it had planned, at a price above its expected range of $70 to $78. An initial public offering (IPO) is the process by which a private company sells shares to the public for the first time by listing on a stock exchange. The company raises money by issuing new shares, and existing owners, such as founders and early investors, can sell some of theirs. To prepare, the company hires investment banks to value it and run the sale. The banks write a prospectus explaining its business, finances and risks. Executives and bankers then pitch the shares to big investors to gauge demand before setting the price. Early investors are usually barred from selling for several months after the listing. Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. It develops AI models under its Claude brand, making most of its money by selling businesses access. Its growth has been extraordinary. In May 2026, Anthropic raised $65bn from private investors at a valuation of $965bn. Its IPO price values the company about 55 percent higher. Anthropic confidentially filed for an IPO in June and made its registration statement public on October 26. Its revenue reached $33.2bn in the first nine months of 2026, including $17bn in the third quarter. That represents rapid growth from the previous year, although the company continues to spend heavily on computing infrastructure. Its November prospectus also reported a net loss of $104bn over the first nine months of the year, largely driven by non-cash accounting adjustments, and disclosed nearly $901bn in computing and infrastructure commitments.  Anthropic overtook SpaceX, which raised $75bn in June by selling shares at $135 each, valuing Elon Musk’s rocket, satellite and AI company at $1.75 trillion. SpaceX’s total rose to $85.7bn after it sold extra shares following its listing. In July, South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix raised $26.5bn when it listed on the Nasdaq, the largest US listing ever by a foreign company. It now ranks third. Saudi Aramco, which held the record before SpaceX, is now fourth. The state-owned oil giant raised $25.6bn on Riyadh’s stock exchange in December 2019, at a valuation of about $1.7 trillion. The rest of the top 10 are Alibaba (2014), SoftBank (2018), NTT Mobile (1998), Visa (2008), AIA (2010) and Enel (1999).          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Anthropic’s IPO surpasses SpaceX, marking the largest initial public offering in US history at $81bn. Save Share Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, is now trading on the Nasdaq through the largest initial public offering in history, surpassing the debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX. The stock began trading on the ticker ANT midday on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) lab, valued at $2 trillion, said last week that it would offer 825 million shares with its initial public offering (IPO) at a price range of $70 to $78 per share. However, that changed on Wednesday when the Dario Amodei-led company announced it would sell 980 million shares at $83 each. By the time the stock ultimately went live, at 11:50am in New York (16:50 GMT), it was trading at $111.50 per share, a 34 percent rise. It dipped below $100 in midday trading, hitting $95.69 by 1:55pm (18:55 GMT). It closed the day at $97.17, still nearly 17 percent higher than its IPO price. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ended the day down 2.2 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down by 2.19 percent and the S&P 500 was down 1.8 percent. Other tech giants also trended downwards, with Microsoft down 1.78 percent, Nvidia tumbling 3.3 percent, Meta down 3.2 percent, Apple by 0.9 percent, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) by 7.72 percent and Micron Technology by 2.1 percent. Anthropic’s high-profile IPO has fuelled excitement across the board, including among industry insiders such as Michael Monaghan, founder and portfolio manager at Founders ETF. “We have indicated our intention to buy in the IPO and hope to get an allocation. The books are well oversubscribed with high-quality orders, according to our trading counterparts,” he told Al Jazeera. Anthropic’s listing is the first of the two major AI labs to go public on US markets, as competitor OpenAI has also eyed an IPO. However, it comes at a rocky time for the AI industry, amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia invested a combined $20bn in Anthropic, including $10bn in a partnership announced in November 2025 and another $10bn in a share purchase tied to its IPO. The massive IPO also comes amid backlash from voters in the recently concluded midterm elections, where all but one ballot initiative restricted expansion of data centres, and a sweep by Democrats who ran on platforms of reining in the AI industry. “Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain,” IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer told the Reuters news agency. That has not dented analysts’ assessments of the sector. “Anthropic’s IPO [is] a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note. Anthropic is also closely watched for how intertwined it is with other tech companies, including Amazon and Google. Anthropic has committed $110bn to Amazon for computing infrastructure over long-term agreements and at least $121.3bn to Google. Anthropic’s Wall Street debut comes amid growing concerns about the safety of its technology. The company’s more than 300-page US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing devoted approximately 90 pages to outlining potential risks, including warnings that its AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. The company also disclosed a net loss of $104bn in the first nine months of 2026 in its SEC filing. The concerns come as a group of AI safety experts has criticised Anthropic in a new statement released in the days surrounding its IPO. Dubbed the “Misanthropic Statement”, it challenges the company’s claims about its commitment to developing safe AI. “Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good,” the statement said. Amid the concerns, the company put out a lengthy statement on the social media platform X. “We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” the statement quoted Anthropic CEO Amodei as saying. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Donald Trump brought Nvidia stock worth $265,000  Nov. 19 2026, Published 3:22 p.m. ET President Donald Trump bought up to $265,000 in Nvidia stock in September, according to a financial disclosure released Thursday, November 19.  The transactions are drawing attention as his administration tightens restrictions on advanced AI chip exports and the technology giant deals with the fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. The disclosure, signed by Trump on November 1 and made public by the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, also showed that he sold up to $15,000 in Nvidia shares during the same month. The figures are reported in financial ranges, meaning the exact transaction amounts are not available. Donald Trump had previously purchased Nvidia shares worth $1.6 million The latest filing follows Trump's August transactions, when he purchased up to $1.6 million in Nvidia stock and sold up to $1 million, according to an earlier disclosure. His September transactions also included purchases of up to $315,000 in SpaceX stock, Reuters reported.  White House spokesperson Davis Ingle previously addressed questions about the president's investments, saying third-party financial institutions independently manage his portfolio and replicate "recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000." Ingle also said investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers, without direction from Trump or his family, Reuters reported.  Nvidia has gained recognition as a maker of advanced AI chips The disclosure comes as the Trump administration moves to tighten controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, including those manufactured by Nvidia. On November 16, the administration announced new export restrictions targeting overseas data centers that provide significant computing power to companies headquartered in China.  The measures cover shipments of advanced chips to Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil. Affected data centers serving Chinese companies will have 90 days to obtain the required licenses.  The restrictions aim to prevent Chinese businesses from accessing powerful American technology through overseas facilities. Nvidia has previously faced pressure over its access to the Chinese market, while Huang had advocated for maintaining sales opportunities in the country. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12, 2026 Nvidia announced on November 12 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately. His departure ended a 33-year leadership run at the company he co-founded.  The resignation followed reports about Huang's personal relationships and concerns involving a possible Chinese intelligence operation.  On November 8, he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, although he did not identify the person involved.  One reported relationship involved Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed.  U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected her of working for Chinese intelligence, but the Justice Department has not concluded that she was a spy. Beijing has also denied the allegations. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.  The New York Times separately reported on November 11 that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. California could face years of staggering deficits running into the tens of billions of dollars within five years if urgent budget repair is not carried out – and the AI boom goes bust.  Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra was issued an urgent warning on Wednesday by legislative analysts, who published the fiscal outlook for the state’s next budget. While the outlook projects California will face a $2 billion shortfall for the upcoming fiscal year, it predicted the deficits are set to soar to at least $15 billion by 2028-29. And in a worst-case scenario, the shortfall could be potentially as high as $30 billion by fiscal year 2030-31.  Advertisement “The problem in the upcoming budget year is relatively small, but it grows to be fairly significant,” legislative analyst Gabe Petek said on Wednesday. Analysts fear an AI bubble could burst the stock market, which is currently propping up the state’s finances with its capital gains tax revenue. Advertisement Analysts said lawmakers have to take that risk seriously. “While the stock market’s recent run has been great for many investors and the state budget, it now appears to have advanced to a dangerous stage,” analysts wrote.  Petek added that the signs of a burst are there: “Every one of these indicators that we’re looking at is the highest they’ve ever been – except for at the peak of the dot-com bubble.”  Advertisement Analysts suggested that the state make $6 billion in cuts or “budget solutions” next year to build up to a $4 billion cushion. Good morning! It's Thursday, November 19, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around. In this morning's edition, General Motors is trying to figure out what its world without Mary Barra in it would look like, over 1,500 Rockstar employees are voting on whether to unionize as Grand Theft Auto 6 goes live, German automakers are staring down the barrel of a work stoppage as a labor fight takes hold and Ford has started shipping the battery cells it's building in partnership with China's CATL. If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here. Mary Barra has been the CEO of General Motors for nearly 13 years at this point. For some, it's hard to think of modern GM without her, but with her 65th birthday just a month away, folks within The General are clearly starting to do so. The automaker is working with an executive search firm to look for possible outside candidates to succeed Barra as it prepares for a future that'll come once the highest-paid Big Three CEO hangs it up. Don't worry, current GM employee, the company is also looking at internal candidates. Barra has apparently been laying the groundwork for months to hand over the keys to the company. She's already GM's second-longest tenured CEO — beaten out only by its first CEO, Alfred P. Sloan, Jr., who was in the position for 23 years. Still, her tenure is about twice that of the average modern CEO of an S&P 500 company, and she's the first woman to run a global automaker. So far, GM hasn't indicated publicly when Barra could step away from her post. From The Wall Street Journal: GM has historically groomed chief executives from its own ranks, and internal candidates remain in the mix. Contenders have included the company's finance chief Paul Jacobson; Sterling Anderson, a high-profile Silicon Valley hire who serves as Chief Product Officer; and Mark Reuss, a 40-year GM veteran and Barra's No. 2, according to separate people familiar with the matter. Barra took over as GM was still rebuilding after its 2009 bankruptcy and has led the Detroit automaker through trade wars, the global pandemic and tumultuous forays into electric and autonomous vehicles. GM's stock, up 25% from a year ago, has risen about 136% since she took the reins, and the company has returned tens of billions to investors through sweeping buybacks. Barra took over with a mandate to shake up the automaker's notoriously hidebound corporate culture. Her GM has emerged as a smaller but more profitable automaker anchored by its lucrative U.S. truck business. GM is selling millions fewer vehicles around the world than it was a decade ago, after retreating from unprofitable foreign markets while slashing low-margin sedans and other slow sellers in the U.S. Yet it is generating record levels of cash and turning bigger profits despite fewer sales. The company has spent the past decade trying to pivot away from its roots as a traditional car manufacturer and instead remake itself into a software-driven tech enterprise—a push marked by a string of Silicon Valley hires, an expanding California hub and heavy bets on autonomous driving and digital services. Of course, not all of Barra's gambles have worked out. GM lost billions on its Cruise robotaxi division before pulling the plug, and its original electric vehicle plans have been a bit of a disaster that cost the automaker $6 billion in write-downs. WSJ also notes that several of the high-profile tech hires it made saw relatively short tenures. Barra and GM are clearly playing things close to the chest. Just a few months ago, the CEO was asked if she's considering stepping down, and she told Fortune magazine that she remains energized. "I still feel like I can contribute and continue to build the foundation," she told the outlet. We'll see how long she continues, but the $48.2 million in realized compensation she made in 2025 certainly helps. Unless you're at Patrick Star's house, you're aware that Grand Theft Auto 6 launched at midnight, and it's one of the biggest video game releases ever. In preorder sales alone, GTA 6 generated over $1.6 billion in revenue, and that number is sure to climb as folks buy it in the coming days. Even with all that immense amount of money, workers at Rockstar, the studio behind GTA, don't think they're getting their fair cut. That's why over 1,600 Rockstar employees in the UK are voting on whether to form a union, and if it wins recognition when the ballot closes on November 26, the Rockstar Games Workers Union would be the largest in the UK gaming sector. In an op-ed for The Guardian, Rockstar animation programmer and union representative Nestor Uriarte said the studio's reason for a unionization push is because of a decade-long realization that "to tackle the industry's mounting challenges we need to come together." He argues that union recognition would help safeguard the working conditions of developers who built GTA 6 over the past decade. From PC Gamer: "Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognized union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to," Uriarte said. "Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too." Working conditions at Rockstar produced one of the early flashpoints in the advancing push for games industry unionization over recent years, sparked by employees' descriptions of its "death march" crunch culture and allegations of sexual assault. While the studio's taken steps towards a healthier workplace in the years since, employees have reported continuing concerns around gender pay gaps, crunch, and nebulous bonuses conditions. Coinciding with the union vote, a Glasgow tribunal is weighing testimonies in the ongoing legal battle around Rockstar's alleged union-busting and firing of employees who had been involved in organization. Meanwhile, just days before a launch that's projected to earn landmark revenue, Rockstar parent company 2K reportedly laid off a third of the employees at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis. "It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off," Uriarte said. "But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised." [...] "We've heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company," Uriarte said. "But we're not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed." Uriarte said that recognition would also provide developers with a greater ability to negotiate the rapid proliferation of AI in game development, which represents an existential threat to workers in an industry where one third of the labor force has been laid off in the past two years. Employees are seeking greater flexibility in labor costs and working hours, and the IG Metall union is pushing for higher pay and commitments to project investment and jobs at domestic factories. KGaA, though the union hasn't identified which sites will be targeted. Watch CBS News  Updated on:  November 19, 2026 / 4:18 PM EST             / CBS News            Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history. Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%. "Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email. Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.  Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday. "The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO. "The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added. San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart. Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added. The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.  Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.  The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to investment bank Renaissance Capital, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).  Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks. Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion. Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading. However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading. Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public. Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News. "I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said. AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors. At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off. "Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note. The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery. "I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday. While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.  As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045. Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test. Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.  Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.  The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.  The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.  The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.  This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.  Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.  Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.  That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

Tokenized Take-Two shares drew $249.5 million in DEX volume Wednesday, nearly three times the $88.1 million for tokenized Nvidia shares. Tokenized shares of Grand Theft Auto VI publisher Take-Two Interactive recorded nearly three times the trading volume of tokenized Nvidia shares on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) as the blockbuster began its global rollout. Trading volume for tokenized Take-Two (TTWO) shares surged 578% to $249.5 million on Wednesday, up from $36.8 million a day earlier, according to Token Terminal data. Tokenized Nvidia (NVDA) recorded $88.1 million in DEX volume despite ranking first by market cap at $399.4 million. The surge made TTWO the most-traded tokenized stock tracked by Token Terminal that day, accounting for roughly 42% of the $590.7 million in DEX volume. DEX trading volume by reference stock on Wednesday. Source: Token Terminal Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based assets that track the value of publicly traded shares, allowing investors to gain exposure through crypto trading platforms. Their onchain trading volumes do not represent transactions in the underlying shares on traditional stock exchanges. Take-Two shares on the Nasdaq rose 6.2% to close Wednesday at $216.61, according to Yahoo Finance. Shares gave back some of those gains Thursday, falling 4% to $208 in premarket trading as of 7:02 a.m. ET. GTA VI, which Citi analyst Jason Bazinet estimated cost about $1.4 billion to make, ends a 13-year wait for a sequel to GTA V. PlayStation and Microsoft’s Xbox both said it was the most preordered game in the history of their respective stores. Most of the tokenized TTWO trading was in a Solana-based asset offered by Backpack Securities, a platform operated by crypto exchange Backpack. The token accounted for about $239 million, or 96%, of the day’s trading volume. Over the past 30 days, tokenized NVDA shares recorded about $2 billion in DEX trading volume, compared with $808.1 million for tokenized TTWO shares. The GTA VI launch has also attracted crypto scammers. Blockchain security company Blockaid said in a Wednesday X post that it had flagged more than 8,800 GTA-themed tokens on Solana as malicious, suspicious or spam, alongside hundreds of social media posts promoting fake airdrops and preorders. Separately, four US senators questioned the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday about potential gaps in investor protections and anti-money laundering safeguards under its new tokenized securities exemption. If Chaka Khan is every woman, Robert Pattinson is every man. He’s Bruce Wayne, Edward Cullen, Antinous, Chris Hansen, and, as of this week, James Bond. The casting announcement is a surprise, and yet not. Pattinson is a man of myriad talents beyond his acting abilities, not least of which is his ability to make seemingly contradictory identities coexist; brooding heartthrob, an indie-film weirdo, a true leading man, a guy who looks like he might sleep in his clothes weeks at a time, and now the international man of mystery (or is that Austin Powers?). Bond is the image of peak male performance, whereas Pattinson is the image of peak male uniqueness. And as gifted an actor as he may be, he’s not necessarily a “commercial” guy. Pattinson is a luxury guy through and through, emblematinc of a major market distinction between the Bond that was and the one that will be. Pattinson’s Bond feels like a tangible step to franchise the feeling of luxury itself rather than luxury products per se. I mean, R-Pattz is the actor with the most preexisting swag to step into the role of James Bond, not least of which because he comes complete with brand deals with Dior Homme and watch company Jaeger-LeCoultre (whereas Bond has historically worn Tom Ford suits and Omega watches). Whereas Daniel Craig’s Bond sold beaucoup peacoats and Barbour jackets without even trying, Pattinson’s feels like it has a chance to avoid selling anything, apart from the idea of being a multihyphenate. Craig’s Bond was the ultimate rugged-luxury man, who wore classically approachable menswear because he was really about that life. Robert Pattinson, meanwhile, is more likely to make the ultimate luxury man look a little more…luxury. Luxury as in, that thing you want simply because it’s so unattainable.  It makes you wonder not just about how Pattinson’s deals will be affected (or not) by Bond-franchise involvement, but whether fans may have a tougher time seeing themselves in a drippier Bond clad in bespoke Dior suits and JLC watches priced akin to family homes in the American Midwest. Pattinson’s appeal is defined by that kind of exclusivity, though. Where Craig’s Bond helped manufacture a career-defining mass-market aura, Pattinson’s swag is already set. From my Zillennial vantage, he arrives at Bond having already been the tortured heartthrob in Twilight with a great head of hair, had a feature on a Death Grips song (he played guitar sample from “Birds”), screwed a mermaid in The Lighthouse, ran from the cops in Good Time, been engaged to and broken up with FKA Twigs, cut his great hair in that weird way, played Batman… This kind of side-quest behavior is itself a luxury; a vibe, rather than a product. Sure, Pattinson has a face that can sell a fragrance campaign (again, Dior Homme partnership), but he’s also the most singular and strangest leading man in modern history, with a pretty epic backstory to go along with it. You could buy any previous Bond’s watch or jacket, but you can’t buy a legacy like Pattinson’s. That’s real luxury. Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a new device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list. While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.  So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 users, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven. Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some big sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much? What makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit. National Amid this week’s announcement that Quebecor is seeking to acquire Telus, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada’s telecom market could become more competitive with fewer major companies under certain conditions. Speaking at a Nov. 18, 2026 press conference in Shenzhen, China, during his visit for the APEC CEO Summit, Carney declined to endorse the proposal or say whether the federal government should permit a telecom market with three major national wireless providers — down from the current four. Quebecor, the Montreal-based owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile, and Fizz, publicly unveiled its proposal to buy Vancouver-based Telus on Nov. 16. The deal is valued at approximately $31 billion, excluding debt, based on the stock prices used in Quebecor’s announcement. When asked by media about the proposal, Carney suggested the effect on competition would depend on how the market is organized. Discussing markets dominated by a handful of large companies, known as oligopolies, the prime minister said that “depending on the market structure, the form of oligopoly can lead to more competition with fewer players under certain circumstances.” He acknowledged that he would likely face some criticism for suggesting this. However, Carney repeatedly stressed that he was not passing judgment on the Telus-Quebecor combined company proposal and pointed to the responsibilities of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission and federal competition regulators. “Again, I’m not going to make a direct comment about the number of players in the market, which would necessarily imply a conclusion about any specific transaction,” he said. A Telus-Quebecor merger would put two of Canada’s four major national telecommunications companies under the same owner, leaving Rogers, Bell, and the combined company. Carney was also asked whether growing competition from foreign satellite provider Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, called for a different approach to the industry. He said the federal government is reassessing telecommunications policy as technology and the market change, while emphasizing the need for companies to keep investing in better services. He pointed to recent rule changes allowing providers to sell broadband services using other companies’ networks, saying that opening up access helps increase competition and lower prices. He maintained that affordability, service quality, and investment would guide the federal government’s decisions. “You need a competitive market structure that provides that competition. We have seen the costs, for example, of broadband come down significantly over the last years, but technological developments, including some of the ones you referenced, has the potential to further that progress,” said the prime minister. When asked about Canadians continuing to face high telecommunications bills, Carney acknowledged that more needs to be done. “There has been improvement, but we need more improvement,” he said. Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with reporters in Shenzhen, China, while attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026. (CPAC) The federal NDP is calling for Carney’s administration to reject the acquisition outright. “We don’t need bigger telecom empires. These companies are already charging us way too much — they don’t need even more power,” said NDP leader Avi Lewis in a statement on Nov. 18. “The Liberal government must not allow this deal to go through.” The NDP leader warned that combining the companies would give a smaller number of owners greater control over the industry and put upward pressure on phone bills. The NDP is also calling for a publicly owned telecommunications option to compete with private companies. Lewis pointed to SaskTel — Saskatchewan’s provincially owned provider — as a model for other parts of Canada. “Only a public telecom option can permanently lower bills and give Canadians a real alternative to corporate price-gouging,” continued Lewis. “Saskatchewan has done it for generations with SaskTel, offering some of the lowest prices in the whole country. It’s time to take that proven model to Quebec and the rest of Canada.” Quebecor argues that combining its networks and resources with Telus would give it more money to improve services and compete with foreign technology and satellite companies. It has also promised to keep Telus’ brands and Vancouver headquarters. The proposal would face intense scrutiny given the federal government’s previous efforts to establish a fourth major national wireless competitor. When Rogers acquired Shaw in April 2023, Shaw’s Freedom Mobile was sold separately to Quebecor’s Videotron. The federal government had refused to let Freedom Mobile’s wireless spectrum licences — the rights to use airwaves for cellphone service — pass to Rogers, instead approving their transfer to Videotron under conditions intended to strengthen competition against Rogers, Bell, and Telus. Quebecor’s new proposal would bring that fourth competitor together with one of the three companies it was meant to challenge. Telus has not accepted the proposal. Its board has raised major concerns about the price, debt, shareholder voting rights, and the likely difficulty of securing regulatory approvals.
